However, important divergences have emerged between cyclical and non-cyclical sectors . Cyclical issuers have generally reduced leverage and maintained healthier margin trends, while non- cyclical sectors continue to exhibit elevated leverage and greater margin compression. While leverage has been supported by strong revenue growth, margins have continued to decline, leaving issuers vulnerable if economic growth slows. At the same time, $HY equity valuations remain elevated , with EV/EBITDA multiples approaching post-pandemic highs. A tighter Federal Reserve policy stance, rising Treasury yields, and persistent inflation increase the risk of multiple compression, which could materially worsen leverage metrics. Furthermore, higher energy costs, rising import prices, and continued cost pressures are expected to drive additional margin compression, especially among consumer-related industries. records.text: We expect industrial demand elasticity to be higher than for power and residential use, although drops in gas demand for power have also been reported in Asia this summer. The question is at what price gas demand destruction would rise, if needed. August trade data suggest that at least 15 mtpa of LNG demand destruction are likely already taking place outside of Europe at current price levels. Our direct conversations with India industrial users of gas suggest $30/mmBtu might be an important threshold to trigger incremental industrial gas demand destruction. Regarding gas-to-oil switching, it’s not something we expect in large scale. While we observed gas switching into oil products in Europe in 2022, this time around distillate fuel prices are also elevated driven by oil product tightness, making it unlikely that natural gas prices can move sustainably above diesel prices (already pricing at 115 EUR/MWh in gas-equivalent terms) to trigger switching. Lastly, we think some gas-to-coal switching might be taking place among China industrial users of gas. This is consistent with LNG usage in industrial applications moving lower year-on-year following the TTF and LNG price rally (Exhibit 5), while China industrial activity has remained robust through August, including in energy-intensive sectors like chemicals. records.text: Rate hikes now more likely than not in November A higher inflation outlook combined with communication this week from the Bank of England leads us to review our expectations for Bank Rate. We now expect the MPC to increase Bank Rate by 25bp at its November meeting and, subject to a continuation of the conflict in the Middle East, a further 25bp in February 2027, leaving Bank Rate at 4.25% (Figure 2). This change of view is motivated by three key factors: (1) the MPC now expects headline CPI to breach 4% in Q1 27, an important threshold; (2) the minutes made clear the committee expects this to lead to increased risk of second-round effects; and (3) individual committee members gave clear, conditional, guidance that if the conflict in the Middle East continues, they would deem it as appropriate to tighten policy further. We therefore judge that, for a majority of the committee, the increased risks of second-round effects now outweigh the continued evidence of slack in the labour market and limited broader pass-through of the energy price shock. For full details see When the facts change, 17 September 2026. Labour market continues to show signs of slack Data this week provided further evidence of slack in the labour market. The Fed raised rates. While inflation continues to show deceleration, the pace of disinflation not fast enough for the FOMC participants. Arguably more important for the call was the Board signalling a higher neutral policy rate, which requires higher policy rates to ensure financial conditions are tight enough to push inflation lower. We therefore see three hikes in this mini-recalibration (Sep, Dec, and Mar). In the euro area, we expect that real growth will continue to be strong, driven by resilient exports and positive public investment - these offset soft domestic private investment. records.text: Japan Macro Watch18 September 2026 ab 2 BoJ raises rates as expected; December vs. January remains a close call As widely expected, the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate from 1.0% to 1.25% at today's Monetary Policy Meeting. This brings the policy rate to its highest level since 1995. The pace of tightening has also accelerated. After raising rates at the June meeting, the BoJ delivered another hike only three months later, compared with its previous pace of roughly one rate increase every six months. In the vote, in addition to Board Member Asada, who also dissented at the previous meeting, Board Member Sato voted against the rate hike. This underscores that both members appointed under the Takaichi administration continue to hold reflationist policy views. There were few significant changes to the policy statement compared with the July meeting. Although the latest hike places the policy rate within the BoJ's estimated neutral rate range of 1.1% to 2.5%, the Bank retained its assessment that financial conditions remain accommodative and that it will continue to adjust the degree of monetary accommodation by raising the policy rate as appropriate. The increase in local bank holdings over recent years has relied on secular tailwinds which we think are now starting to fade. First, loan-to-deposit ratios in Poland have been on a secular decline since the end of the 2007–2008 financial crisis and are now bottoming out just above 60%. This has expanded the role local banks play in the domestic bond market, with government securities making up 26% of the domestic banking system's assets – the highest share on record (Figure 11). The other tailwind has been a continued tightening in the spread between the interest rate on new corporate loans and POLGBs, which has also made POLGB holdings more attractive for local banks (Figure 12). records.text: ab 18 September 2026 Global Research Japan Macro Watch BoJ hikes, but no strong case for December yet BoJ raises rates as expected; December vs. January remains a close call The BoJ raised its policy rate from 1.0% to 1.25% at its September meeting, as widely expected, bringing rates to their highest level since 1995. With the hike coming only three months after the June move, the pace of normalization has accelerated. The statement was largely unchanged, maintaining that financial conditions remain accommodative despite rates having entered the estimated neutral range. Governor Ueda struck a broadly neutral tone. Although he refrained from providing explicit guidance on the future path of rate hikes, he stated that the phase of monetary policy has shifted from raising inflation to stabilizing inflation around the 2% target, while reiterating the risk of an inflation overshoot. At the same time, he suggested that consecutive hikes or 50bp moves would likely require a significant inflation overshoot, limiting immediate hawkish implications. Looking ahead, the meeting did not provide sufficient evidence to decisively bring forward our next hike call from January to December. The timing remains finely balanced between those two meetings, although a renewed bout of yen weakness could strengthen the case for a December move. At the same time, investment is weighed down by the prolonged property downturn, retrenchment in capital expenditure across traditional industries, tighter local government finances, and weaker incentives for local officials to pursue aggressive infrastructure expansion. Banks representing around 25% of EA banking assets reported that they are close to their preferred reserve level (see ECB blog). This number is expected to broadly double by the end of 2026. Therefore, as a result of the MRR increase, there will most likely be a mix of banks rebuilding their HQLA buffers - for example by retaining or acquiring government securities, or by raising term funding - and banks rebuilding their reserve holdings - for example through repo borrowing or through ECB refinancing operations. After an MRR increase, secured funding and >2-year unsecured issuance become relatively more attractive than short-dated unsecured funding, as they do not add to the MRR base. The redistribution of reserves is also likely to increase, and repo markets' rates are likely to see some upward pressure, especially as repos have a zero MRR coefficient. Banks close to regulatory liquidity targets are increasingly using term money markets, which has pushed up premia on term liquidity (see here). The increase in MRR could accentuate this momentum. records.text: Product cracks need to stay elevated to ration both end-user demand and restocking demand. We expect 2026 to be another year of negative net capacity additions in ex-China refining markets as potential ~0.3mb/d capacity additions is more than offset by ~0.6mb/d capacity closures (Exhibit 1). This tight capacity backdrop, combined with the historical utilization context, highlights why product cracks likely need to stay elevated for longer: the refining system cannot accommodate a full demand rebound in 2027 and meaningful restocking while keeping refinery utilization at normal, sustainable levels (Exhibit 2). If 2027 product demand were to recover to 1% above 2025 levels while the market also attempts to rebuild half of the 2026E product inventory draw, the required refinery runs would push utilization into unprecedented territory, which we do not view as operationally realistic. In practice, the adjustment mechanism is therefore likely to be price-led: high cracks need to suppress both end-user demand and inventory restocking demand enough to bring refinery utilization back toward a feasible range. Using the highest utilization level observed over the past five years as a guide for feasible operating limits, we estimate that a potential combination of 2027 demand at 1% below 2025 levels and no inventory restocking in 2027 would be needed to bring the refining utilization back toward that range (Exhibit 3). records.text: 2. Clients’ view: No winter supply optimism, TTF and JKM on their way up. Market participants overwhelmingly expect no change to the status quo in Persian Gulf LNG exports, and expect this will drive winter TTF and JKM prices higher towards our 105 EUR/MWh (TTF) and $35/mmBtu (JKM) upside price scenario. Our take: 105 EUR /MWh TTF is not our base case (which is lower, at 70 EUR/MWh), but it is our expected peak winter price should Persian Gulf LNG supply lack (Exhibit 3). To be clear, while geopolitical uncertainty remains elevated and we make no assumption of a lasting Iran deal, our base case assumes a gradual market adaptation in LNG supply, though slower than what we have observed in the oil market. Persian Gulf LNG exports have averaged between 15% and 25% of pre-war levels over Jul-Aug, and our base case assumes a gradual export ramp to two-thirds of normal, already a reality for oil, by January 2027. This more cautious approach by LNG shippers likely reflects the risk of transporting a fuel that generates a higher heat level when burning than that of oil, and the technical challenges of executing LNG ship-to-ship (STS) transfers outside of the Strait of Hormuz1. Importantly, military attacks in the region continue to pose a risk that Persian Gulf LNG exports take even longer to ramp. Although core goods inflation has picked up since the start of the year, this largely reflects the one-off effects of Germany's healthcare reform and higher information and communication equipment prices linked to the global AI cycle. Services inflation, meanwhile, remains well behaved, with the pre-conflict trend of wage moderation intact for now. Looking ahead, several factors will shape the euro area inflation outlook over the coming months and quarters. Beyond the trajectory of energy prices, which in our forecasts remains conditioned by futures curves, a key question will be the extent to which higher energy costs are ultimately passed through to end consumers. We expect evidence of such indirect effects to become increasingly visible in the period ahead, as pipeline price pressures, already apparent in PPI and import price data, gradually work their way through the production chain (Figure 7). The extent of this pass-through will depend not only on input costs but also on demand conditions and firms' pricing power. While survey evidence, including the PMIs and the ECB's Corporate Telephone Survey, suggests that firms have so far absorbed part of the increase in input costs, the resilience of economic activity leads us to expect firms to renew efforts to rebuild margins. The OIS curve is now pricing a terminal rate close to 3.4% by end-2027, with little expectation of rate cuts further out. Given the current macroeconomic backdrop, this appears excessive and our assessment rests on several considerations. First, we continue to think that a majority of Governing Council members view the current shock as predominantly supply-driven. Even if the euro area economy has proved more resilient than expected, it is not overheating because of excessively strong demand. According to the latest European Commission estimates, the output gap remained negative at around -0.2% of GDP in 2025 and, with growth expected to run close to or only modestly above trend over the next six quarters, is unlikely to close before the end of 2027. records.text: ab 21 September 2026 Global Research Global Economics & Strategy Core Convictions (Multi-Asset Rundown) All our views on markets in a single page This 'core conviction' document is our weekly one-page multi-asset rundown where we highlight key events in the week ahead and any view changes (see page 2). Highlights this week Although market pricing remains well below the tightening we expect from the Fed (one further hike in December), ECB (one in December) and BoE ( November and February), we are wary of calling the peak in rates given the uncertain energy outlook. We continue to favour relative-value over directional duration trades, including US 2y forward 2s10s steepeners, while taking profit on our inflation swap steepeners. In Europe, we expect further inversion of the ESTR curve (target: -10bp in 2s10s) and favour receiving SONIA 1y1y versus 6m1y on the view that tightening will be reversed relatively quickly. We continue to believe middle distillates will remain structurally tight through 2027 given low inventories, limited global refining capacity additions and a persistent geopolitical risk premium. European refiners coverage is particularly well positioned, with c.45-50% of product yields exposed to diesel and jet fuel. records.text: Banks and AI: A Credit-Positive Outlook In June, we reviewed earnings transcripts and regulatory filings across investment-grade non-financial corporations in the USD and EUR credit markets. Our key takeaway was that, while management teams increasingly frame AI as a productivity opportunity, evidence that these benefits are materializing at scale remains limited. We also argued that the AI buildout is becoming a major driver of corporate funding needs. AI-related issuers have already contributed meaningfully to debt supply this year, and we expect the funding burden to broaden as more firms finance their own AI capex. Reflecting this dynamic, we recently raised our 2026 USD IG gross supply forecast to $2.3 trillion from $2.1 trillion and penciled in $2.4 trillion for 2027, setting the stage for two consecutive years of record gross issuance. This week, we turn to banks. Our review of earnings calls, regulatory filings and transcript data across the largest investment-grade US and European banks suggests that AI is credit-positive for the sector through two channels, which directly inform fundamental metrics: Fee generation and ecosystem lending: Banks can capture advisory, debt and n equity underwriting, and syndication revenues from the AI capex cycle while generally limiting retained long-dated infrastructure risk. UK inflation forecast update Restrictiveness required Headline CPI accelerated to 3.1% y/y in August, driven by increased pump prices. We update our medium-term inflation outlook for higher energy prices and our revised view on Bank Rate. We expect CPI to average 3.1% in 2026 (+0.1pp) and 3.0% (+0.5pp) in 2027. • August headline CPI was 2bp above our nowcast, but in line to 1dp, accelerating by 0.2pp to 3.1% y/y (3.09 at 2dp). Compared to our published forecast (see Ofgem price cap to increase 4% q/q in Q4, 26 August 2026), the print was the same as our forecast to 2dp, with core inflation 7bp lower, printing at 2.6% y/y (2.57% at 2dp). Underlying services held broadly steady although momentum increased, offset by more volatile components of services disinflating. For a detailed analysis of the print, read Much the same, much changed, 16 September 2026. • The energy outlook has materially worsened, with no clear signs of a near-term improvement. Energy prices in wholesale markets have risen in recent weeks, in particular for gas, which has a more meaningful impact on the UK inflation outlook. As crack spreads remain high and oil prices have shifted higher, we now expect auto fuels inflation to surpass 30% y/y in September. records.text: 18 September 2026 Fixed Income Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 How has each EGB spread performed relatively to other countries? Instead of using PC1 from other risky assets like we did earlier, now we use the average EGB spread as the only explanatory variable. Hence , this is an intrinsic valuation exercise with the sum of residuals adding up to zero, i.e. for every outperformer there has to be an underperformer. The benefit of zero -sum residuals outweighs the cost of the fact that each individual country spread (Y - side variable) is also impacting the average EGB spread (X-side variable). After all, this impact is small due to averaging across 9 different country spreads. It’s no surprise that the chart below looks very similar to the chart above since the average EGB spread is currently only 2bp cheap relative to other risky assets as shown in Figure 1. Nonetheless, the split between the three main underperforming EGB spreads, i.e. OATs, BTPs & OLOs, vs the rest is a bit clearer in Figure 4 due to the zero-sum element of this analysis. It’s also interesting that the BTP residual has been range -bound since March, different from Figure 3 – a sign that the recent cheapening is part of the broader EGB spread weakness and not an idiosyncratic cheapening move like for OATs & OLOs. Regional activity is surprising to the upside, with South Korea and Taiwan reporting double -digit nominal growth and benefiting most from the surging semiconductor cycle. Technology i s the common growth engine, but domestic value capture remains the key differentiator, with ASEAN running a large trade deficit with China. Monetary policy responses are characterised by broader rate hikes, although their timing varies, as inflation rises to 3.2% in 2026 from 1.7% in 2025. High oil prices, El Niño and rising US rates pose shared risks. (Please refer to the Sept AMI for details.) In North Asia, South Korea’s "fiscal push, monetary pull" dynamic is notable, as a massive semiconductor tax windfall funds aggressive fiscal expansion, leaving the BoK to do the heavy lifting in containing inflationary pressures and financial risks. After a brief pause in October, the BoK will likely deliver three more 25bp rate hikes in response to above -potential growth and broadening housing price inflation. records.text: 1. Banks Outpace Non-Financial Issuers in AI Mentions AI has become an increasingly important theme in bank earnings calls. On average, AI was mentioned roughly nine times per US bank call and four times per European bank call in Q2 2026 (Exhibit 1). Banks have consistently discussed AI more frequently than non-financial firms since 2025H2, coinciding with the broader adoption of more advanced AI models. On a sector basis, US banks ranked behind only technology, excluding hyperscalers, in terms of AI mentions in Q2. European banks ranked behind technology and communication services (Exhibit 2). However, there remains meaningful dispersion across firms. In the US, nearly every bank in our sample mentioned AI at least once, with the largest banks mentioning AI the most (Exhibit 3). Conversely, in Europe, several smaller European banks did not raise the topic at all. We present in Exhibit 8 different levels of multipliers and the associated interest expenditure savings. In theory the ECB could calibrate the multiplier so that the decrease in the interest bill is enough to cover the increase in the interest expenditure on the back of the increased policy rate. For example, to cover the additional interest rate expenditure associated with 50bp worth of rate hikes, the multiplier would need to be set at least at 2x (covering €352 billion) bringing a reduction of €8.8bn in interest rate expenditure. For the set up to cover 75bp worth of rate hikes, the multiplier would have to increase to at least 3x and to cover market pricing of policy rate rising to 3.25%, we would need to see the multiplier set at 4x. But this is not where the story ends. Redistribution of excess liquidity would likely take place, resulting in (much) lower interest rate expenditure relief than planned for. The higher the multiplier, the higher the incentive for banks to trade "reverse allowances" (as observed during the two-tier system). We expect an additional 25bp hike at the December meeting, with rates then staying on hold at 2.75% until end-2027. Risks are skewed towards the need for additional rates increases should the energy outlook fail to normalise. • Fiscal concerns are back in focus, with France at the centre of attention. Following Prime Minister Lecornu's latest announcements, we have revised up our deficit forecasts for both 2026 and 2027, to 5.4% and 5.5% of GDP , respectively. Based on Markowitz’ Modern Portfolio Theory the optimal bond weight in a balanced portfolio is a function of (1) relative return, (2) relative risk, (3) diversification benefits and (4) the return on cash. With higher equity/bond correlations the optimal bond weight decreases, and that means lower Sharpe ratios and higher portfolio volatility. The optimal bond allocation also decreases with better relative equity returns vs. bonds and higher relative risk. Higher returns on cash can also drive a higher equity allocation as bonds become less attractive vs. cash. Growth and demand pressures are just not there in the Euro area. Similarly, the BoE remained on hold this week. And while we see risks of a hike by the BoE rising, we think any tightening is unlikely to be the start of a prolonged hiking cycle. In contrast, the market is pricing almost 100bp of hikes despite limited passthrough to core so far, softer labor market backdrop, and restrictive rates. And it was pricing even more before the BoE held rates this week. In Canada, BoC communication surprised on the hawkish side focusing more on headline inflation. But with relatively weak growth, elevated trade uncertainty likely to weigh on investment, and core inflation still at target, is hard to envision the BoC hiking in tandem with or more than the Fed in face of the oil shock. Despite central banks not having the best track record on inflation since the pandemic, it is one thing to argue that neutral rates may have increased, but it is a different thing to argue for interest rates to go back close to the peaks of the cycle. Another leg higher in oil and refined products would likely put renewed upward pressure on the expected policy path, back- end yields and bond volatility. The symmetry with 2024 is worth noting: cutting the policy rate then did not ensure lower long-term financing costs; today, raising it need not ensure higher long-term nominal financing costs, particularly if doing so reduces longer run inflation uncertainty. In short, stocks have valuation support here, and earnings remain strong. We remain convicted in our year-end S&P 500 target of 8,000, though we acknowledge rising crude and refined product prices as the primary near-term risk to the index. Should the correction in valuation take a turn for the worse in the near term due to a further tightening of financial conditions and/or materially higher energy prices (the near-term risk scenario), we think the S&P 500 could trade as low as 7100 before the bull market resumes into year end. This follows a Merton model framework, where a sharp de-rating of equity valuations creates incentives for shareholders to restructure the business, typically to the impairment of credit holders. The median EV/EBITDA of $HY issuers continues to grow higher , approaching post-Covid highs. records.text: US Economics Weekly18 September 2026 ab 6 Once interest costs become large enough, balancing the primary budget is no longer sufficient to balance the budget overall; a primary surplus is needed merely to reduce debt while continuing to meet interest payments. Further consolidation in the early 1990s under President Bush, including tax increases and tighter discretionary spending, eventually returned the primary balance to surplus by 1995, helping to stabilize debt relative to GDP , and allowing interest costs to decline, falling below 2% by the early 2000s. Today’s starting point is more difficult. The primary budget deficit is projected to remain near 3% of GDP in the coming years and has not recorded a surplus since 2007. Debt held by the public is expected to surpass its previous postwar peak of 106.1% of GDP by 2029 and exceed 120% by the end of the 10-year budget window. (3) Under the higher- rate scenario, it could reach 126% of GDP by 2036. The danger is not simply a larger interest bill: persistently higher rates could set off a self-reinforcing cycle in which greater debt raises interest expense, larger interest expense widens deficits, and wider deficits add still more debt, crowding out other spending and leaving policymakers with progressively less room to respond to the next downturn or crisis. records.text: Global Rates Strategy18 September 2026 ab 3 GBP covered bond issuance is enjoying a standout year, with supply already exceeding GBP20.6bn YTD. This not only surpasses the GBP15.4bn issued in FY2025 but also exceeds the nearly GBP20bn recorded in 2023, previously the strongest year on record. While the GBP covered bond market has traditionally been dominated by UK issuers, accounting for around 46% of annual issuance on average since 2015, the main story this year has been the resurgence of Canadian issuers. Canadian banks have issued around GBP8bn, matching UK volumes, doubling their GBP4bn total for FY2025, and approaching the historical peak set in 2021. More broadly, the pass-through from higher energy prices into core inflation has so far remained relatively narrow. We think the limited transmission reflects the widespread expectation that energy price pressures would prove temporary and be resolved in the short run. That perception is likely changing. Absent a resolution this year, firms may begin to treat higher transportation and input costs as more persistent. As a result, we expect broader pass-through into core prices to emerge over time, particularly in early 2027 when many firms typically implement annual price resets following the holiday season.

Israel's relatively low dependence on oil further cushions the economy from energy price shocks, with natural gas accounting for more than 70% of the energy mix and renewables approximately 16%. The structure of fuel pricing provides an additional buffer, as excise taxes and VAT together account for roughly 55-60% of the retail gasoline price. While this does not insulate the economy entirely from global energy shocks, it reduces the sensitivity of domestic prices to fluctuations in oil markets. Moreover, following a further increase in gasoline prices in September, the Ministry of Finance temporarily reduced the fuel excise tax to limit the pass-through to consumers. If Brent prices remain elevated through YE27, the effect on macro variables will depend on shekel dynamics (significant appreciation, which could potentially result from the election outcome, would offset this) and geopolitics (risks of renewed escalation with Iran). records.text: Oil Services Tenaris (TENR.MI, Neutral): Tenaris has been present in Venezuela for many years, and currently supplies Chevron OCTG needs in the country. Tenaris has long-term relationships both with current players like Chevron, ENI and Repsol, and US majors that could potentially increase its presence in the country (XOM and COP). In addition, Tenaris owns a local office (service center) in Venezuela, and TuboCaribe facility in Colombia which includes 105kt of welded pipe manufacturing capacity and a 250kt seamless pipe finishing plant. This might provide a logistical advantage to Tenaris to expand business in Venezuela. Vallourec (VLLP .P A, Buy): Vallourec delivered OCTG to Venezuela in the 1990s and currently does not have presence in the country. The company used to supply premium OCTG solutions from a technical standpoint (sour service casings/13Cr or CRA tubings for corrosive/high temperature/high pressure conditions). These pipes were previously supplied from Vallourec’s European mills. Today, with production concentrated in Brazil rather than Germany, Vallourec could benefit from a significantly more competitive cost base and logistics chain. Venezuela OCTG market would require complex higher-premium OCTG solutions. Rather, it is now adding upward pressure on consumer prices – although probably neither the size nor the duration of this effect will be enough to raise serious concerns about inflation overshooting . We would not read a potential change in the SNB’s language on currency interventions as a signal for incoming rate hikes. The outlook beyond this week OIS markets price in roughly two 25bp rate hikes by the SNB meeting in June 2027. While uncertainty is elevated, we struggle to reconcile this market pricing with Switzerland’s current inflation outlook. We believe it is more likely that the SNB will keep rates steady at 0 .0% throughout 2027. Although inflation rates should come in higher in the years 2026 -2028 than the SNB projected three months ago, we expect them to settle at a bit below 1% in the medium term, well within the central bank’s target range . In our base case, the SNB therefore does not need to raise its policy rate to keep inflation in line. records.text: Lastly, we use a purely statistical (GARCH) approach to estimate how much “vol premium” is embedded in the surface. Volatility tends to cluster – high vol begets high vol and low vol begets low vol – making past volatility a useful predictor for future behavior. We predict volatility one month ahead using a set of these models with different lookback periods to avoid anchoring to a vol regime too far back. We then average their signals and compare this aggregate forecast to the current market implied volatility. If implied volatility is significantly above the model forecast, it typically corresponds to higher subsequent vol selling returns2. While this approach is more rudimentary, it offers another angle on how expensive vol is. 2 We use a 1y, 5y and full sample (since 2000) lookback window and estimate a GARCH model for each on daily changes in the respective tenors, averaging the signals from the different approaches. We then map 1m subsequent returns to each percentile of that aggregate signal. In turn, we revise upward our 2027 GDP growth forecast from +4.8% to +6.5%. We have also expanded our range of forecasts to now include the rest of the Gulf economies (Figure 2). Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain have been hit hardest this year due to their greater reliance on the Strait of Hormuz for exporting hydrocarbon products. In addition, hydrocarbon revenues make up a larger share of state revenues and this, in turn, has caused budget and current account positions to deteriorate sharply, requiring larger fiscal adjustments and creating a headwind to non-hydrocarbon activity. In contrast, the UAE's economy should only experience a minor downturn as its exit from OPEC+ has allowed for oil production to go beyond pre-war levels and its access to the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline has allowed for oil exports to navigate around the Hormuz closure. Finally, Oman will be the sole GCC economy to expand in 2026. Our view is that underlying inflation has been stuck around 2.5% for several quarters because policy isn’t tight enough to push it back to 2% (Exhibit 2). Moreover, we think the resilience of the economy changes the Fed’s risk/reward calculus. On the one hand, it presents Warsh with an opportunity to make a stronger push to get inflation all the way back to target, without risking a recession, than Powell’s Fed was willing or able to do. This seems to be a stroke of good fortune, and we think Warsh is doing the right thing by seizing the moment. On the other hand, robust nominal growth increases the risk that if the Fed doesn’t tighten, demand-driven inflation could pick up as the supply shocks fade. Will three hikes be enough to get inflation back to target? Our base case of a modest 75bp hiking cycle is premised on our view that i) the underlying inflation overshoot is also modest (50bp), and ii) supply disruptions should roll off the y/y rate in coming quarters. To answer that, we take a look at what demand has done in response to the increase in prices so far this year. The OECD, China and India together account for roughly two-thirds of global oil demand. While there is little policy interference in the OECD, Chinese demand can be hard to gauge, and in India, the government tries to largely insulate consumers from sharp price increases. But in aggregate, the mix is a decent representation of global demand. The recent gradual recovery in Chinese oil demand from the lows in Q2 26, despite few signs of a coincidental recovery in economic indicators, suggests that the demand slump in Q2 26 was likely more indicative of the pull-forward in Q1 26 and potentially even Q4 25 than a simple reaction to higher prices. Therefore, it probably makes more sense to look at H1 26 demand as a whole rather than just focusing on Q2 26. In H1 26, Chinese oil demand was down 840 kb/d y/y, based on our estimates. According to the IEA, OECD oil demand fell 570 kb/d y/y over the same period, while in India, oil demand was up 120 kb/d y/y in the first half of this year. Taken together, demand from the three was down 1.3 mb/d or 1.9% y/y (Figure 3). EUR supply growth broadens beyond France and Germany Despite the strong increase in overall EUR covered bond issuance this year, the two largest jurisdictions, France and Germany, have lost market share. Having each accounted for around 21% of total EUR covered bond supply in FY2025, Germany's share has fallen to 19% in 2026 YTD, while France's has declined more markedly to 17%. In contrast, Canada has increased its share from 6% to 11%, while both Spain and Italy have seen their share rise from 3% to 5%. A regional breakdown tells a similar story. While Western Europe remains the dominant source of EUR covered bond issuance, accounting for roughly EUR120bn of the more than EUR170bn issued this year, issuance from the region is around 4% lower than in FY2025. By contrast, all other regions except Japan/Australia/New Zealand have recorded strong growth, ranging from 31% to 80%. North America, which in practice equates to Canada, has posted the strongest increase, with issuance up 87% versus FY2025. The data suggest that this year's surge in EUR covered bond supply has been driven less by the traditional core markets and more by peripheral European and non- European issuers, while newer covered bond jurisdictions such as Hungary and Israel continue to broaden the market's issuer base. The updated September Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) was more hawkish than expected. FOMC participants revised up GDP growth forecasts for 2026-27, lowered projected unemployment rates, and nudged up inflation forecasts, with median PCE inflation not expected to return to 2% until 2029. Policymakers also continued to view inflation risks as skewed to the upside. The revised dot plot signaled broad support for further tightening, with the median participant expecting one additional 25bp rate hike this year, holding rates in 2027 at 4.00-4.25%, and then cutting 25bp in each of 2028 and 2029. The longer-run policy rate was revised up to 3.25%, suggesting that the FOMC no longer views current rates as clearly restrictive and sees a higher neutral rate than previously assumed. Essentially to get to 2.0% inflation the median participant had a funds rate path 50 bps higher in September compared to June. records.text: US Economics Weekly18 September 2026 ab 13 effect" on the monetary policy decisions. He sounded like higher rates would have no impact on the labor market expansion. "I don't believe that we need to do harm to the labor markets to achieve our objective. I don't believe that the two parts of our mandate, price stability and full employment, are working at cross purposes over the medium term," he said. He rattled off a range of observations about financial markets and credit, all of which were justification for tighter monetary policy. His assessment of financial conditions appeared to be a clear signal he thought more rate hikes would be necessary. How many is unclear. His 18 colleagues in the dot plot think only one more is appropriate this year, and only four saw a need for a hike at both of the next two meetings. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 18 September 2026 3 After all, inflation is stuck above target, but not even close to the post-pandemic peak, and the overall economic background is much more balanced. The labor market is in balance rather than extremely tight, wage growth is more contained, a small negative fiscal impulse is expected for next year, and underlying inflation is below 3%. Keep your feet on the ground In our view, markets are overpricing rate hikes across much of G10. 100bp of hikes in the US is a risk scenario that could potentially happen, but market dislocations seem even larger in other markets. The US is characterized by remarkable resilience, less sensitivity to the energy shock, solid consumption growth, and the AI capex boom. There are possible paths leading to a larger hiking cycle, but our base case is for 75bp in total. In comparison, if we take the case of the Euro area, the UK, or Canada, market dislocations appear much larger. Since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in late February 2026, inflation in Poland has accelerated by 1.3pp to 3.4% y/y, leaving it just below the upper bound of the NBP's inflation tolerance band of 3.5%. Higher energy prices accounted for 1.1pp of this increase, despite government measures aimed at limiting pass-through via lower fuel excise duties and VAT rates. At the same time, food inflation remains unusually low, at -0.9% y/y, compared with a five-year average of 8.3% y/y. This appears increasingly difficult to sustain, given adverse weather conditions, higher energy and fertiliser costs, and rising global food prices. Against this backdrop, and with domestic demand still operating close to potential, we expect inflation to rise further, to 4.2% y/y, by YE26, before moderating to 3.0% y/y by YE27. The corporate health version of backward looking when forward driving Our corporate health measure moved into “vulnerable” territory in 1Q26, when the data included only one month of the energy price shock. Actual credit origination was still ok in 1Q26, but perhaps that represented lagged demand, or corporates drawing on credit lines amid inventory or working capital needs during the energy price shock. Rising funding costs could yet show in loan dynamics. National accounts-based profitability measures could provide some 2Q relief. But that metric focuses on labour costs. The unemployment rate stayed unchanged at 4.9% 3mma, but we expect it to increase next month, based on the single month values and leading indicators on employment (for more on the labour market data see First Look: July Labour Market, 15 September 2026). Looking ahead, the more restrictive policy path we now expect will weigh further on the labour market, and we have revised up our unemployment rate forecast for 2027 by +0.3pp to 5.7%, although 2026 remains unchanged at 5.1%. This softer labour market outlook is one of the offsets in our inflation forecast that limits the upward pressure on core CPI from recent energy moves. GDP growth lower in 2027 as energy and rates bite Tighter monetary conditions, alongside a more intense and persistent terms-of-trade shock also lead us to revise down our growth outlook. Positive signs of growth over the summer months continued this week, with retail sales in August growing 0.5% m/m. There has also been a positive trend in the Q2 and July GDP data in investment and activity related to technology and seemingly AI innovation. We expect this to continue, with business investment resilient in our forecast even with higher interest rates. However, private consumption is likely to be sensitive in the first half of next year to a bigger real income squeeze and tighter financial conditions, which are already biting even before the BoE has raised rates. records.text: 21 September 2026 Global Economics Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 6 Oil Crude flows: Brent prices are up by more than a third since the early August low after the Houthis entered the conflict, having declared a Red Sea blockade. This has resulted in a serious impact to Saudi Red Sea shipments as well as a September halt to the Petroline (East-West pipeline) operation that feeds the refinery and port of Yanbu. Offsetting this, export flows through the Strait of Hormuz have been improving more than vessel tracking data might suggest. The US Centcom has been providing security to ‘dark’ transits (with AIS turned off) along the Omani coastline, and vessels subsequently perform ship -to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Because the vessel ultimately delivering the oil is different from the one origina lly loading it, tracking data may not capture these flows. Supply accommodation: Both the US and China are providing less cushion for global markets facing supply constriction. The US is returning to its pre -conflict pace of crude oil net imports as SPR withdrawals abate (although refined product exports remain above normal), and Chin a has begun raising its refinery runs and crude import rate from the June lows as refinery crack spreads have improved. Note that 9% (~10 mmb/d) of global refining capacity is located in Gulf countries. Market pricing: As a result of oil redirection, supply reduction has been limited to 8.5 mmb/d yoy in Q2-Q3’26. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 21 Sep 2026 08:08:27 ET │ 15 pages US Economics Inflation Weekly – Will rising diesel costs push up goods prices? CITI'S TAKE We were surprised to see the median core PCE forecast in the September SEP rise to 3.4% from 3.3% in June. We think it is likely that most Fed forecasts do not include upcoming revisions and that core PCE will ultimately be lower than many officials are expecting this year. We continue to track core PCE around 3.0-3.1%Q4/Q4. A renewed substantial increase in energy prices has caused fresh concerns about pass-through to core inflation, particularly as elevated diesel prices mean higher transportation costs for various goods. But recent historical evidence is limited about the correlation between higher diesel prices and core goods in CPI. We are still hesitant to conclude there will be substantial pass through as long as real income growth remains soft. Market rents have picked up slightly in recent months but remain softer than pre-pandemic, suggesting shelter inflation should continue to slow. Persistent and Common Component of Inflation (PCCI) is one of the measures of underlying inflation monitored by the ECB. PCCI aims to capture common developments across different items in the consumption basket representing the more persistent part of inflation. PCCI is constructed using a generalised dynamic factor model, where a common factor is estimated across 12 eurozone countries and around 1000 monthly price series. The PCCI is then calculated as the weighted average of the estimated common components. Using this approach the PCCI should exclude short-term volatility due to temporary/transient factors and reflect medium- and long-run movements in inflation. See detail, Bańbura and Bobeica: PCCI – a data-rich measure of underlying inflation in the euro area , ECB Statistics Paper Series, October 2020.

records.text: One shortcoming of this model, however, is that some of the inputs – surveys from Consensus Economics – are slow moving and can thus be slow to adapt to rapid shifts in fundamentals. Using the signals embedded in a suite of macro assets is a complementary approach we have shown can help in this regard. We extract the principal components from a collection of macro markets and use the factor loadings to identify a growth factor and a policy factor. From the combination of the momentum in each factor, for example dovish policy momentum combined with weak growth pricing, we can classify each moment in time into percentiles of changes in policy stance and growth pricing (Exhibit 5) 1. As above, we then find the average returns in the months following each percentile to get a sense of which backdrop is associated with better or worse subsequent vol selling returns. We find that on average the best returns to vol selling come following sharp positive repricing of the growth outlook alongside easier policy. Conversely, weak growth momentum, typically leads to worse subsequent returns (Exhibit 6). 1 We apply principal components analysis to daily normalized changes in a set of 18 market variables. Based on the factor loadings and the correlation with yields, breakevens and equities we then label them as a growth or policy factor. It is hard to argue with the notion that the labor market has been “stable” and that economic growth has been “resilient. ” But we do not see strong evidence for a nascent acceleration. Regarding the labor market, payrolls strengthened in August, but that report followed much weaker than expected readings in June and July. 70k average jobs per month over the last three months is a solid pace given a slow growing labor force, but is significantly weaker than job growth was originally reported earlier this year. The unemployment rate has been stable around 4.1%, but this is partly due to a drop in the labor force participation rate. records.text: itics, Economy and AI The meeting itself is an achievement. Despite the last-minute preparation, we think a reciprocal state visit carries heavy symbolic weight: it keeps “constructive strategic stability” well in place, which markets should welcome, avoiding the tariff-led volatility experienced last year. Should President Trump and President Xi meet again around APEC and the G20, they would have met four times in 2026 alone — an unprecedented cadence, in contrast to just one meeting between President Xi and former President Biden under the previous US administration. We expect the agenda to span trade, AI and geopolitics, with incremental but concrete progress rather than a “grand bargain” . We believe the most likely deliverable is an extension of the trade truce, covering tariffs, rare earth export curbs, and agricultural and aircraft purchases, alongside progress on operationalizing the bilateral Board of Trade (Bo T) and Board of Investment (BoI) agreed in May. The two sides could also set up a formal US-China AI dialogue to manage national security risks, as Secretary Bessent has signaled (CNBC, Sep 20). Hawkish hold The Bank of England (BoE) kept the Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75% with a 6-3 vote as expected. It highlighted little evidence of material second round effects so far, along with soft labour market conditions and tightening in financial conditions weighing on inflation. But there was a decisive hawkish shift compared to July, as we expected, in light of recent energy price moves. We interpret today’s decision as signalling that the BoE looks closer to moving towards tightening if the recent rise in energy prices is sustained and barring big downside data surprises. Overall, the BoE is getting increasingly nervous about sitting out this shock entirely. records.text: et rates; 2) bank lending; and 3) asset prices. We continue to expect quarterly hikes to a terminal of 2% Overall, we thought Ueda’s press conference remarks were balanced. The Governor did not explicitly commit to maintaining a quarterly pace of hikes and set a high bar for back-to-back moves. At the same time, he stressed the need to steadily reduce policy accommodation now that underlying inflation is near the target and risks are tilted to the upside, thereby avoiding larger, more disruptive hikes later. Given this, we remain comfortable with our call for quarterly hikes, with our base case for the next move at the 17-18 December MPM (see BoJ Watch: Faster hikes, higher terminal, 14 August 2026). The dovish dissents by the two Takaichi-appointed Board members are a reminder that the Takaichi government’s cautious stance toward rate hikes remains the biggest source of uncertainty, and the main risk to continued BoJ normalization. However, we do not think this precludes continued quarterly hikes. Any resurgence of expectations that government pressure could delay BoJ hikes would weaken the yen. Moreover, with inflation set to pick up strongly in the coming months (see Back to school: Can’t have it all, 11 September 2026), we think it will return to the spotlight as a political issue, softening the government’s stance. The greater uncertainty comes after July 2027, when the terms of the two hawkish BoJ Board members, Takata and Tamura, expire. - Izumi Devalier & Takayasu Kud

A more hawkish Federal Reserve, which has already resumed its tightening cycle, is likely to affect the region unevenly. While these divergent policy paths have resulted in varying spreads relative to the fed funds rate (Figure 5), countries' sensitivities to Fed monetary policy also differ (For whom the Fed tolls). LatAm central banks are increasingly following their own paths. They acted in unison when COVID hit. Nevertheless, there was some loss of correlation in the post-COVID hiking cycles, probably as the epidemic ended at different times in different places, given how quickly they got vaccines, but afterwards there has been an even lower correlation between their monetary cycles and the US Fed's (Figure 6). In the most recent cycle in Latin America, central banks that did not face threats to their credibility (Chile, Peru, and Mexico) were able to ease and are now on hold, whereas those where such threats, among other issues, interrupted easing cycles and forced hikes are now either easing again, as in Brazil, or are potentially closer to beginning an easing cycle, as in Colombia. This time might be different. In our view, this time it will be a function of how the FOMC implements rate hikes. records.text: EEMEA Outlook Contained for now, but vulnerability ahead The macro effect of the energy price shock has been limited in EEMEA so far, with higher energy CPI largely offset by easing food prices and stable FX. records.text: M Idea 2 Goodbye disinflation, hello oil risk premium We make several changes to our outlook for the US economy this week. First, we revise modestly higher our inflation forecast through the end of 2027 on account of recent trends and persistently higher energy prices. Inflation is stickier: it still decelerates, but more slowly than before. Second, we nudge lower our outlook for growth in 2027 and marginally soften our outlook for the labor market. Stickier inflation and tighter financial conditions mean less broadening out of the expansion. Third, we pencil in two additional 25bp rate hikes from the Fed in December and March, bringing the target range for the federal funds rate to 4.25-4.50%, which we expect to remain in place through the end of next year. These changes shift us away from our previous disinflation outlook into an "oil risk premium" baseline. We adjust the probabilities of our alternative scenarios accordingly (see Exhibit 31 for more on the alternative scenarios). Moving away from benign de-escalation Our mid-year update to our outlook for the US economy assumed a benign de-escalation scenario in the Middle East conflict. Along with payback from tariffs and other forces, a resumption of lower oil prices would help inflation decelerate, broaden the expansion, and keep the Fed on the sidelines. In the June edition of our Emerging Markets Quarterly, we expressed greater comfort around the Middle East conflict's negative economic growth impact on Emerging Asia, especially given the sustained boost from the AI boom. We maintain that sanguine view amid the latest re-escalation. Our estimates indicate output gaps generally retreated in Q2 as they felt the fuller impact of the Middle East conflict – but remained relatively solid on average, especially for the key semiconductor supply-chain nodes in the region. Into Q3, the latest available trade data for Emerging Asia suggest the region's export cycle has picked up further from already elevated levels. The AI boom remains a significant driver of this strength, with most major nodes in the region's tech supply chain still enjoying a visible lift to electronics exports. That AI-driven strength in exports will likely keep policymakers in Emerging Asia from sinking into excessive morosity over the GDP growth impact from the latest re-escalation in the Middle East conflict. The BoJ continues to signal vigilance toward the risk that underlying inflation may overshoot its 2% target. At the same time, the Bank may have deliberately avoided stronger guidance, as explicitly signaling a faster pace of tightening could unnecessarily constrain its future policy flexibility. In our view, Governor Ueda's press conference was broadly neutral. As in the past, he refrained from providing explicit guidance on the pace of future rate hikes, or the eventual terminal rate. However, he stated that "the phase has changed," explaining that the policy challenge has shifted from raising underlying inflation toward ensuring that it remains stably anchored around 2%. He also reiterated the risk of an inflation overshoot. Because markets had already priced in a highly hawkish outlook, with the implied probability of a December hike exceeding 80%, some participants may have interpreted his remarks as relatively dovish. Despite opposing forward guidance, Chair Warsh delivered on what he signaled at Jackson Hole, which we saw as an overcorrection for his July presser. Our view has been that rate hikes were necessary in the US, and Warsh stated many of the reasons that we have argued: loose financial conditions, strong growth, the capex boom, a solid labor market, and inflation that remains too high. We expect the Fed to deliver an additional 50bp of hikes in October and December. In turn, the market is already pricing the hiking cycle close to perfection, absent any further shocks, with about 75bp of additional hikes. In contrast, the share of items posting year-on-year price increases of more than 2% for at least 12 consecutive months has risen to 19% on a weighted-average basis. This is substantially higher than the average level recorded in 2021, before inflation began to accelerate in earnest. Although the indicator has edged down recently, it remains above the levels observed during late 2024 and 2025, suggesting that the number of items undergoing gradual but sustained price increases continues to grow. The service sector deserves particular attention. Restricting the analysis to service items reveals an even clearer upward trend in inflation persistence. While service inflation itself has been moving broadly sideways, the share of service items recording price increases above 2% for more than one year has continued to rise steadily. This divergence likely reflects differences in the pricing mechanisms between goods and services. Goods prices are more susceptible to external factors such as import costs, resulting in frequent fluctuations that can temporarily push inflation rates below 2%. Taking stock of these considerations, our central forecast sees headline inflation accelerating to around 4% in the coming months before easing progressively from early 2027 and moving back towards target-consistent levels by Q4 27, helped by favourable energy base effects. We expect core inflation to rise to around 2.8% by March 2027, driven primarily by core goods prices, while services inflation should remain broadly stable around 3%. Food inflation is also set to become an increasingly important driver of the inflation outlook next year. We expect it to strengthen materially over the course of 2027, reflecting the cumulative effects of energy pass-through, the 2026 heatwaves and other adverse supply shocks, including those linked to El Niño, ultimately pushing retail food inflation back above the 3% mark. On an annual average basis, we project euro area inflation at 3.1% in 2026 and 2.8% in 2027, with core inflation at 2.4% and 2.6%, respectively. The BoJ also appears to be more concerned about the risk of underlying inflation overshooting 2%, driven by more aggressive corporate pricing behavior and rising inflation expectations, than about the downside risks to economic activity stemming from higher oil prices. Governor Ueda cited the rise in medium- to long-term inflation expectations during the April-June quarter as one of the key developments since the July meeting. Given the recent increase in oil prices, inflation expectations are likely to remain elevated for the time being. That said, we continue to view market expectations for a terminal rate above 2% as overly aggressive. In our view, the cumulative effects of the rate hikes already delivered, the still subdued pace of growth in private-sector service prices within the CPI basket, and the potential drag on economic activity from higher oil prices all argue against such a high terminal rate. The BoJ is likely to carefully monitor indicators such as bank lending growth, financial institutions’ lending attitudes, and the impact of higher interest rates on small and medium-sized enterprises. However, some of these indicators are lagging in nature. We therefore believe that an overly rapid pace of rate hikes could raise the risk that underlying inflation in 2027 falls short of the BoJ’s current projections.

The tendency for implied volatility to embed a premium over realized on average allows for positive returns to systematic vol selling strategies, as we have shown in the past. Delta-hedged short gamma strategies – i.e., selling short-dated swaptions to harvest this premium – are profitable when subsequently realized vol is lower than what was implied ex ante. We have presented different valuation metrics to identify the characteristics of environments in which vol selling tends to perform best. Here we put them together to generate an aggregate signal for when the time is right to sell interest rate vol. Our first approach is a fundamental macro fair value model. Our framework uses forecast uncertainty across growth, inflation, and the short rate and uses controls including the level of yields, the size of the Fed’s balance sheet, and mortgage convexity to help us benchmark the average level of implied volatility across the surface. Across different specifications, we get a model-implied fair value range (Exhibit 3). We find that deviations from the mid-point of the fair value range, especially when large, or even outside the range, tend to be useful predictors of future returns, with a hit ratio of around 70% of predicting the sign of the one-month ahead vol-selling returns (Exhibit 4). Given the country now has a revised point target of 3% with a +/-100bp tolerance band around it, we believe that the authorities may have to re-engineer a less-accommodative stance in order to build their characteristic credibility into the new regime. Unfortunately, inflation has been drifting further and further away from the new target since its official adoption in November 2025 (CPI only printed at 3% once, in February 2026). In addition to inflation, we believe that the current account will likely come under pressure too. For now, buoyant gold and platinum prices are helping to offset the negative impact of higher oil prices. However, we note that the world has never been able to tolerate oil prices well above the USD100-120/bbl mark for more than a few years without sinking into recession. Were sticky oil prices to eventually trigger a global recession in which commodity prices also come off the boil, South Africa’s current account deficit could weaken meaningfully, with significant implications for the currency. records.text: Economics On the economics side, the new fiscal regime (c.56% government take under LOH 2026) has materially improved project-level economics with an oil breakeven of c.$58/bbl, placing Venezuela in the 2nd quartile of the cost curve (below the 50th percentile at $64.5/bbl). Venezuela’s gas breakeven of c.$3.8/mcf (peak-weighted across Perla, Dragon and Loran) places it in the 2nd quartile of the gas cost curve (below the 50th percentile at $4.3/mcf). The transformation in Venezuelan project economics runs entirely through the new fiscal package under the Ley Organica de Hidrocarburos (LOH). Under the reformed LOH 2026, the fiscal framework is built around two new contract types. The CPPH (Contrato de Produccion y Participacion de Hidrocarburos) applies to ENI at Junin 5 - a 25-year contract with 25% royalty and 35% income tax, with ENI as exclusive operator. Chevron’s revised JV agreements at Petroindependencia, Petropiar and Petroboscan carry enhanced fiscal, commercial and legal terms which management describes as supporting total costs below $20/bbl, a c.$35/bbl breakeven and a >50% IRR at $70 Brent. On an NPV-at-15% basis, we see the largest value in Venezuelan assets for Chevron ($6.4bn), ENI ($4.8bn) and Repsol ($1.9bn), with potential Dragon/Loran FID derisking further value for Shell ($0.3bn) and BP ($0.1bn). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 is to increase MRR from 1% to 2%, according to a Reuters article from July. This discussion is not new. Connected to the review of the operational framework in 2024, we had expected the ECB could increase MRR to 2% (and with that back to 2012 levels). We saw this decision as one possible compromise, given that there were also reports of proposals to increase MRR to 3-4% (see here). Yet, in the first leg of the Operational Framework Review in March 2024, the ECB decided to keep MRR unchanged at 1% (see here). An increase in MRR would effectively work like a tax on banks, unlikely to be entirely neutral to the transmission of monetary policy. In fact, the July 2023 ECB accounts showed that some members raised caution against using the MRR ratio as a policy instrument. We expect this argument will have considerable weight this time around too. In addition, a number of Governing Council members have been on record confirming that they are not concerned about the losses posted by the individual NCBs or the ECB (see Lagarde, Nagel, and Lane). If the Council is not fully convinced about the motivation and has reservations about the proposed methods, we would still remain cautious whether the ECB will really go ahead with the increase. BEI Curve: The Tax Trough Is Confined to Two Bonds The highest-conviction driver of the BEI curve is the proposed two-year reduction in the food consumption-tax rate from April 2027. A cut from 8% to 1% would lower covered prices by 6.5% under full pass-through. The relevant component is food excluding fresh food, dining out and alcoholic beverages, with a weight of 1,756, or 18.3% of the ex-fresh-food CPI basket. The resulting drag on ex-fresh-food CPI is 1.18ppt. Fresh food is also covered by the tax cut but excluded from the index used for JGBi indexation; the 1.38ppt effect on headline CPI must therefore be distinguished from the 1.18ppt effect relevant to JGBis. The transmission to the index ratio is mechanical. April 2027 CPI becomes the reference index on 10 July 2027, while a reversion in April 2029 would enter the index on 10 July 2029. The trough is therefore confined to reference-index dates between 10 July 2027 and 10 July 2029. Mapping this window onto redemption dates shows that only two bonds mature against an index in the trough (Figure 6). Issue 22 redeems against December 2026 CPI and matures before the trough begins. records.text: While low-volatility and high-dividend stocks have lagged the broad market since the COVID-19 crisis, they have performed better relative to the market excluding Tech. And in Tech-driven equity drawdowns, like the Deepseek sell-off in Q1 2025 and the momentum unwind in July 2026, they materially outperformed. In fact, the proportion of stocks with a negative beta to the market has increased sharply, very similar to the Tech Bubble (Exhibit 7). As we recently wrote, this is in large part due to the growing Tech and AI dominance in equity benchmarks – after the Tech Bubble burst, low volatility and high dividend yield stocks were also up, with S&P 500 down 46% and the TMT sector down 79% (Exhibit 8). This was in part because they benefited from lower bond yields, but even during the 2022 drawdown without a large decline in bond yields, they managed to outperform materially. The market has already fully priced in such a move, leaving Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference as the key focus. In assessing the future rate hike path, we believe it will be important to monitor: (1) how the BoJ updates its rationale for raising the policy rate beyond 1.25%; (2) how it intends to balance the need for nimble rate hikes with the assessment of their cumulative impact on the economy; and (3) what stance it adopts toward the unusual series of comments by senior US government officials during the G20 period regarding USD/ JPY and Japan’s monetary policy. The market is currently pricing a terminal rate of around 2.2%, but we believe the hurdle is high for the BoJ to deliver communication sufficiently hawkish to fully validate those expectations. The press conference—no date, but back-to-back hikes and 50bp "not ruled out" The Governor said the Bank "will continue to raise the policy rate" to achieve the 2% target in a stable manner, and stressed that "the phase of policy has changed" from one in which the Bank had hiked cautiously while guarding against downside risks to prices. On the cadence, asked whether he had a particular interval in mind, he said "no"; on the possibility of hiking at two consecutive meetings or by 50bp at once, he said that "depending on price developments, no particular approach can be ruled out", adding that hiking appropriately reduces the risk of being forced into large hikes later. There is no date, but the option to accelerate has been left explicitly open—in our scenario terms, a press conference standing on the line between A (cadence left open) and B (an acceleration signal). On the terminal, he said that "the degree of accommodation is gradually shrinking" after 1.25% but that "accommodative financial conditions will be maintained"; the neutral rate (the Bank's estimated range is 1.1–2.5%) is "a concept and a variable that is hard to pin down" and the terminal rate "hard to identify", signalling reluctance to judge whether policy is restrictive by reference to the neutral rate. Rising r* expectations should be met with hikes Third, some clients have asked us why the Fed should care about the spike in long-end yields (which we view as part of the reason for hiking). After all, breakeven inflation and term premia have remained contained, suggesting markets aren’t worried about Fed credibility (Exhibit 4). In our view, the increase in real yields suggests markets are pricing a higher path for real policy rates, consistent with expecting a structurally higher policy path I.e., a higher r*. We agree that this isn’t as worrying for the Fed as de-anchoring of inflation expectations would have been. But it doesn’t absolve policymakers from the need to raise rates either. records.text: US Economics Weekly18 September 2026 ab 5 Higher rates mean trillions more in fiscal costs Since the Congressional Budget Office's most recent deficit projections earlier this year, the bond-market sell-off has lifted U.S. interest rates by roughly 80 basis points across the curve. On an ordinary debt load, that move would be painful. On today’s federal debt load, that could be transformative. If rates remain near these levels, the government’s interest bill would rise sharply. That hits just as net interest costs are already near a record share of GDP , total public debt now tops $40 trillion, and debt held by the public stands above 100% of GDP , about twice its 50-year historical average. Plus, deficits were already expected to be above 6% of GDP the next few years. The arithmetic is stark. The CBO’s February baseline assumed that the 10-year Treasury yield would average 4.1% in 2026 and roughly 4.3% over the projection horizon. The 10-year yield is now around 5% after briefly pushing above 5% for the first time since 2007 this week. Applying the CBO’s published rules of thumb, a persistent 80-basis- point shift higher across the curve would add about $3.1 trillion to net interest costs from 2027 through 2036 and widen cumulative deficits by roughly $2.5 trillion relative to the February baseline. Given the scale of the July improvement, however, both the new orders and shipments indexes remain at the upper end of the recent range. FRBNY services survey weakens in September The FRB of New York's services sector survey indicated contraction in September after strengthening in July and August. The headline business activity index fell 9.2 points to -8.7 in September, near in line with its June level before an 18.8-point gain in July lifted the headline index above zero. The business climate index, which has signaled contraction since July 2021, fell 10.2 points to -35.9 in September. AI Disruption Concerns Have Shifted Towards Cyber Risk Finally, earlier this year, banks faced increased scrutiny over concerns about AI-driven disruption to bank business models, including faster deposit repricing or lower customer switching costs. However, these now appear to have subsided in earnings-call discussions (Exhibit 10). Within risk disclosures, only one major bank identified structural business-model disruption as a material AI risk. Even then, the concern was primarily the risk of falling behind peers in AI adoption. Instead, cyber and operational resilience have become the more prominent focus areas vis-à-vis potential AI-related risks (Exhibit 11). Banks are increasingly focused on the potential for AI-enabled cyberattacks, fraud, software vulnerabilities and operational failures. This also appears consistent with the growing supervisory focus on AI-related operational and cyber risk. For instance, the ECB has directed significant institutions to submit formal remediation plans addressing AI-enabled cyber risks, information and communication technology (ICT) governance, and operational security weaknesses. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 13 COVA: Cross-Asset Correlation-Valuation Framework Our correlation-valuation (COVA) scorecard aims to identify good portfolio diversifiers at reasonable prices, rewarding assets that have: 1) a more negative correlation to equities, 2) a more stable correlation, 3) a more negative downside beta, 4) more attractive valuations, and 5) more attractive carry. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 18 September 2026 7 We flag that the new ECB-BIG credit conditions index1 also supports our concern that the credit deterioration being driven primarily by prices rather than quantities. The index points to a renewed tightening in corporate financing conditions since the start of the Iran conflict, with the worsening largely concentrated in price-related components, notably lending rates. In other words, the main challenge for corporates currently appears to be the rising cost of credit rather than an outright lack of access to financing. That said, SAFE survey evidence suggests that this pattern may not persist indefinitely. While firms on aggregate reported broadly unchanged availability of bank loans in 2Q26, the picture was markedly weaker for SMEs which continued to report a deterioration in credit availability and a widening financing gap (Exhibit 7). By contrast, large firms reported an improvement in access to bank credit. This divergence is important because tighter pricing conditions often translate into quantity restrictions with a lag, particularly for smaller and more bank-dependent firms. The deterioration in SMEs' perceptions of credit availability therefore suggests that the transmission of tighter financing conditions may already be underway, even if aggregate credit origination has remained relatively resilient so far. Although appreciation pressures on the Swiss franc have eased somewhat over the summer, with the CHF down 3.3% YTD in real effective terms, we do not anticipate a return to the pre-March wording (namely a "willingness to be active in the foreign exchange market as necessary"). Our base case remains that the SNB stays on hold until 2028, in contrast to market pricing. First, the data tends to be volatile and one quarter is insufficient to establish a trend. Two potential factors spring to mind: first, this national accounts definition mainly measures profitability relative to labour costs. Energy prices play only a very limited and indirect role. As a consequence, increased profitability at the very start of the energy shock may reflect the differential between aggregate prices and sticky wage growth, rather than a more underlying improvement. Profits could still compress meaningfully if corporates are unable to pass on the energy bill to end consumers. Second, much of the Euro area improvement in national accounts-implied profitability seems to be driven by German manufacturing improvement and French stabilisation. Increased German manufacturing profitability in late 2025 may have been a genuine improvement helped by job shedding and hence lower labour costs. records.text: Operating practice in Venezuela has settled around horizontal wells with extensions of 1,000-2,000 meters as the preferred procedure as of 2021 (link), which is compared to >3,000 meters in the US shale (10,000 feet). We therefore assume 300-400 tons OCTG per well, 40% lower than in US shale horizontal wells. Using the assumptions above, we arrive at 140-240 kt of OCTG demand in Venezuela by 2030. With premium OCTG solutions ranging from $3,000 to 7,000/t, we assume a $4,000/t OCTG price and arrive at $0.6-1bn total OCTG market size in Venezuela by 2030. The current addressable OCTG market size for Tenaris and Vallourec is 5.7 mn t and c.$18bn, on our estimates, which implies the Venezuela market could add 3-4% to their addressable demand in volume terms and 3-5% in dollar terms given potentially more premium pricing (necessary due to the primarily high-sulfur and heavy crude in the country). records.text: from our client conversations. Near-Term Market Views 1. Clients’ view: Europe winning cargoes from Asia – for now. US suppliers confirmed that they are currently sending most of their flexible cargoes to Europe instead of to Asia, though LNG sellers in Asia pointed out that some buyers in the region are returning to the market after postponing their LNG import demand during the August TTF and JKM rally. Our take: Both observations are consistent with recent volume and price data (Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2). While the Asia spot LNG price premium relative to European gas prices (JKM-TTF spread) remains low enough to continue to incentivize US LNG supply to head to Europe instead of Asia, it has recently pushed against the threshold that might flip that delivery incentive (red line in Exhibit 2). Should Asia LNG demand strengthen enough under current price levels to take the JKM-TTF spread above the cost for US exporters to divert cargoes from Europe to Asia, this would signal increased competition for LNG cargoes and, as a result, would pose upside risk to our TTF and JKM forecasts, both in our base case and upside price scenario. While Chair Warsh presented a relatively unified message, we expect a more nuanced range of views to emerge, particularly on the balance between cooling inflation and labor market risks. The remarks will help gauge whether support for the current policy path is as broad as recent messaging suggested or whether meaningful differences remain beneath the surface. Preliminary September PMI surveys are expected to continue signaling solid economic growth, with strength in both manufacturing and services activity Durable goods orders should move largely sideways at high levels after a year of strong business investment supported by AI-related spending and tax incentives. In housing, new home sales are likely to stay subdued as higher mortgage rates and elevated inventories weigh on demand and prices. Meanwhile, jobless claims are expected to remain historically low, underscoring limited layoffs, though seasonal distortions around Labor Day could generate near-term volatility in the claims data. We expect that the CBC will eventually join others in hiking rates later in the year in response to firm CPI inflation, rising housing prices and broadening growth. In ASEAN, the MAS led the tightening cycle and appears to have room for one more move in October , given its 4.5–5.5% growth outlook. After 100bp of hikes, growth concerns have deterred BI from tightening further, but risks linger , while fuel subsidies strain Indonesia’s strict 3% deficit limit. The BSP is also likely to refrain from further hikes until Philippine growth improves, but a weak peso driven by low real rates could force its hand. Despite strong growth, rates were kept steady amid relatively benign inflation, but price pressures will rise ahead, prompting BNM to hike in early 2027 . Thailand continues to recover amid sustained FDI interest and strong exports, but concerns over high import content have kept the BoT dovish, with no rate hikes likely through year -end, although changes are likely in 2027. Finally, Vietnam is tracking nearly 9% growth in Q3 as the SBV prioritises growth and uses liquidity management rather than policy rate adjustments to address stability risks, although the dong remains at risk and structural bottlenecks persist.
