records.text: Fed Hikes to Slow, Rather than Derail, the Gold Rally We maintain our $5,400/toz end-2027 forecast despite yesterday’s Fed hike and our economists now expecting an additional hike in October. While higher rates should continue to weigh on gold prices through ETF demand in the near term, our economists expect the Fed to deliver three cuts between September 2027 and March 2028, leaving the terminal forecast unchanged at 3.25-3.5%. We therefore expect the impact of tighter monetary policy to be felt primarily through a slower near-term appreciation path rather than a lower terminal gold price (Exhibit 1). We nevertheless continue to expect gold prices to grind higher in the near-term and now estimate year-end fair value at $4,650/toz (below our previous $4,900/toz forecast but above the current spot price of roughly $4,350/toz), as much of the expected tightening already appears priced into ETF demand, stronger-than-expected central bank purchases continue to offset the remaining drag from higher rates (Exhibit 2), and call-option demand for gold as macro policy hedge has proven resilient. records.text: 6 Adapting to a changing climate in the management of coastal zones 1) Built Environment & Infrastructure Resilience There is a growing shift in both public and private capital allocation toward climate-resilient infrastructure, particularly in areas such as flood defences, storm water management and the hardening of critical assets. Companies operating in this space play a central role in enabling system-level risk mitigation by combining engineering expertise with climate modelling capabilities. • Construction materials offer a direct way to gain exposure to adaptation. Higher average temperatures, floods and wildfires are accelerating demand for fire-, water- and heat-resilient materials, creating growth opportunities for companies providing durability-enhancing solutions across the built environment. Cool roofs, advanced insulation and high-performance facades help reduce cooling demand while improving resilience, supported by rising retrofit activity, tighter building standards and growing urban cooling needs. • Coastal protection is becoming a long-term structural investment theme. With ~40% of the global population and 75% of the world's largest cities located in coastal regions6 , demand for sea walls, storm-surge barriers, shoreline protection and nature-based resilience solutions is set to rise as governments and asset owners seek to protect infrastructure exposed to sea-level rise and flooding. The OIS curve implies a 60% chance of a hike in October and additional hikes afterwards, to a terminal rate near 3.4% by end-2027. This appears exaggerated, in our view. First, the ECB's early policy reaction and consistent communication regarding its reaction function vis-á-vis the energy price shock has provided it with a credibility buffer. This makes back-to-back hikes (ie, one in October) very unlikely. Absent a further significant shock, the ECB will likely want to stick to its quarterly path at meetings when it updates its forecasts (ie, December). More fundamentally, the inflation shock remains largely supply driven. Although growth has been more resilient than expected, the euro area economy is not overheating. European commission estimates still show an output gap in 2025, which even with the current modestly above-trend growth should leave some spare capacity well into 2027. Hence, there is no need for an aggressively restrictive policy stance, especially as persistently high energy prices will increasingly weigh on households and businesses over time. 18 September 2026 5 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: Hawks high on energy

Revising mortgage rate and origination volume forecasts Following forecast revisions by our economics and rates team, we now revise our 2026 and 2027 mortgage rate and origination volume estimates. The clearest example and our biggest revision is the Fed. While for much of the year, we had thought the Fed would avoid hiking rates, now in addition to the increase at the September FOMC meeting, we now expect two additional rate hikes, in December and March, bringing the terminal rate to 4.25-4.50%. While Chairman Warsh highlighted the inflationary implications of higher energy and commodity prices, the more important signal was their assessment that policy is still not be sufficiently restrictive. Although Chair Warsh said that he does not think that a neutral rate estimate is helpful in making policy decisions, he nevertheless described the September move as "removing a dose of accommodation," and the rest of the FOMC did (albeit very slightly) revise up its estimate of the neutral policy rate. In our view, the Fed appears to be reassessing not just the inflation outlook, but the amount of restraint required to bring inflation sustainably back to target. Still, we see the shift as more of a recalibration rather than a fundamental shift in policy, so the market may have over estimated how much hiking is left. There were also discussions in 2022 to introduce tiering to recoup the additional unintended stimulus provided to banks on the back of the TL TRO III favourable pricing formula (see our analysis from then here). History of a two-tier system: The two tier system was a mechanism introduced in October 2019 to reduce the cost that negative interest rates imposed on euro-area banks holding excess reserves at the Eurosystem. A portion of each bank’s excess reserves was exempt from the negative deposit facility rate and instead remunerated at 0%. The exemption was initially set at six times the bank’s MRR. It was effectively suspended in September 2022, once the ECB moved away from negative policy rates. Calibration is challenging: As we already argued in 2022, a sound calibration of a tiering system would be very difficult and every option brings its own challenges. Page 2 Overview We enter the autumn with the global economy staying resilient in the face of renewed geopolitical escalation and energy risks, in part thanks to the ongoing AI investment boom. This resilience coupled with rising risks of inflation persistence have led to a broadening of the global rate -hiking cycle. A key question is how long activity can absorb high energy costs , rising rates and constrained fiscal positions. The risk is that tighter policy eventually bites more forcefully as higher yields or a correction of AI-related equity valuations tightens financial conditions. The energy shock has moved back to the center of attention in recent weeks, with supply concerns rising amid an escalation between Houthi fighters and Saudi - backed forces in Yemen, coupled with the ongoing Iran -US stand -off. Both Washington and Tehran appear to be waiting for the other to blink, and resolution does not appear imminent, though political pressure on the Trump administration may ramp up closer to the midterm elections. Improving flows through the Strait of Hormuz provide some offset to the disruption to Saudi shipments via the Red Sea, but abating SPR withdrawals in the US and stronger Chinese refinery demand leave less cushion, while the loss of Gulf refining capacity and curtailment of Russian supply keeps product markets vulnerable. records.text: 4 This includes: floods, storms, heat stress, droughts, wildfires, water stress, and sea-level rise Heat stress adaptation highest In terms of perils addressed, adaptation products and services most often help protect against floods, storms, heat stress, drought, wildfire, water stress, sea-level rise and general extreme weather events 4 . Within our universe of companies, a higher share of companies provide products that help combat heat stress (Figure 6). This likely reflects the growing impact of rising global temperatures and the increasing frequency, intensity and duration of heatwaves, which are creating significant challenges for infrastructure, energy systems, water resources and economic productivity. As a result, a wide range of adaptation solutions are focused on enhancing resilience to heat- related risks. These include resilient public and private infrastructure designed to withstand higher temperatures; cooling technologies and thermal management systems; heat-resistant building materials and building envelope solutions; and resilient electricity grids and distributed energy systems that help manage rising cooling demand and maintain reliable power supply during heatwaves. records.text: On a 6-12m horizon, the case for higher bond allocations would strengthen if growth slows materially or AI-driven earnings tailwinds fade. For now, strong earnings growth still favours equities over bonds: prospective global equity carry - which combines the starting dividend yield plus the subsequent change in earnings - has increased sharply YTD supported by the AI investment boom, and our equity strategists still expect slower but still strong earnings growth in 2027. This should keep equity risk-adjusted returns attractive versus bonds, even as relative returns moderate. We remain OW equities, N bonds and UW credit on a 12m horizon. Over longer horizons, higher starting yields should lift optimal bond allocations from the unusually low levels of the past five years. Higher yields improve carry and medium- to long-term buy-and-hold returns, while providing more cushion against further yield increases. This strengthens the case for higher strategic bond allocations than in the past 5 years, when bonds had limited value in portfolios, but mainly reflects a normalisation back towards the long-run optimal range of 35-55%. However, even over 10-year horizons most of the variation across possible long-term scenarios is driven by equities, similar to the near term. The MPC judged the shock as looking protracted with most members placing more weight on energy prices staying higher for longer in the absence of a lasting de- escalation. Near term energy prices are close to the BoE’s adverse scenario, though less persistent. While the BoE has seen little evidence so far of material second round effects, it noted that risks of material second round effects have increased since July and it was possible that indirect effects from energy on inflation had just been delayed rather than diminished. There was also increasing mention of risks of inflation exceeding thresholds where attentiveness to inflation has typically increased, especially in the run up to 2027 wage setting round (which previous comments from BoE has suggested is close to 4%). More importantly the BoE highlighted that “Given the lags with which second-round effects appeared, it was not appropriate to wait too long for evidence of such effects before responding with policy”. At the same time, the MPC raised its near-term inflation forecasts to 3.75% in 2026 Q4 and slightly above 4% in 2027 Q1 based on energy futures as of 14 Sept. That comes on top of the current net interest expense of the federal government which is already at all-time highs. Productivity and Operating Efficiency Take Center Stage When discussing internal AI deployment, we found that banks focus primarily on efficiency gains through automation, as well as cost control. Management teams often bundle AI initiatives with broader digital transformation and IT modernization programs, with this theme more pronounced in the US than in Europe (Exhibit 8). records.text: US Economics Weekly18 September 2026 ab 10 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Week in Review: a hawkish hike The FOMC raised the target range of the federal funds rate 0.25 pp to 3.75% to 4.00%, as expected. There were no dissents, and the median assumptions of appropriate policy revised higher. The Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) showed the median participant assumes another 0.25 pp rate hike will be appropriate this year, and that it would be appropriate to maintain that 4.1% midpoint of the target range throughout 2027. The FOMC left the nominal policy rate at 3.6% at the end of their forecast horizon in 2029 while inflation returns to 2.0%, suggesting that the FOMC is acting like a funds rate over 3.5% would be needed to ensure that outcome. After this week's international airfares data from the import price data, we expect core PCE prices rose 0.27% and headline PCE prices rose 0.32% in August. Alongside, the annual revisions from the BEA include methodological changes to PCE prices which bring more uncertainty than usual to these estimates. We estimate the annual revisions will lead to a downward shift in core PCE inflation from 3.34% in July to around 3.18% in August, and headline PCE inflation we expect moved down from 3.70% in July to 3.56% in August. We have revised up our inflation trajectory to reflect higher energy prices and a one-off increase in healthcare costs in Germany. Underlying inflation broadly stable in August, but expectations tick up The final Eurozone HICP estimate for August (published 17 September) was revised slightly lower to 3.2% from 3.3%. The increase was driven entirely by higher energy inflation, while underlying inflation metrics broadly pointed to stability. records.text: ab 21 September 2026 Global Research US Daily Data Recap Fed speakers support September hike The first Fed speakers coming out of the September FOMC meeting broadly argued that inflation remains a broader-based problem than just energy prices. FRB of Kansas City President Schmid argued that inflation excluding energy has " been running hot" and FRB of Minneapolis President Kashkari noted that price pressures are evident " in all aspects of the economy ," especially services. Similarly, FRB of Chicago President Goolsbee argued that persistent supply shocks cannot simply be " looked through," while suggesting some inflationary pressure may be coming from "overheating demand ." Together, remarks in the past few days supported the September rate hike, with Schmid noting that the Fed has "work to do" on inflation and the hike was a "step in that direction." We noted in this week's US Economics Weekly that a regime shift could be underway (link here). Ahead of President Trump's meeting this week with Chinese President Xi in Washington, Secretary Bessent met over the weekend with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng. We think that the ECB will most likely discuss the excess liquidity remuneration measures around the October monetary policy meeting. The measure is still topical given the ECB raised rates again in September (to 2.5%) and we expect it to do so again in December (to 2.75%). The interest rate bill of the ECB (and therefore a payout to banks) has increased by approximately €9.0 billion per year (based on 2027 forecasts for excess liquidity and 50bp worth of rate hikes). Since the P&L consideration is one of the main reasons behind the revival of the MRR increase discussion, we expect the motivation for a discussion have only strengthened. Since our last note on MRR at the beginning of July (following the first Reuters article), another Reuters article emerged suggesting that the ECB might be alternatively considering tiering as a measure to lower its interest rate expenditure bill. records.text: 21 September 2026 US Credit Strategy Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 7 How much is improved $HY rating quality worth? Zooming out, much has been made of the improvement in the $HY market's rating quality in recent years. $BBs make up a record share of the $HY index at 56%, while $CCCs now account for just 10% of the index. That is the lowest share of $CCC bonds since 2002. In total, the average rating of the $HY market is now the highest it has ever been (Figure 11). There are multiple drivers of this rating quality improvement. 1) the $HY market has looked to finance higher quality issuers in recent years as $LL and private credit have financed riskier debt. 2) A greater sum of subordinated-debt from $IG rated issuers. 3) A few substantial Fallen Angels over the last two years have introduced significant $BB debt into $HY. records.text: China Outlook Turnaround remains elusive Domestic demand deteriorated further. Structural drags continue to weigh on consumption and investment. We maintain our below-consensus 2026 growth forecast of 4.5%, with downside risks. President Xi's visit to the US will be the main focus next week. Following weaker-than-expected credit demand, August activity data reinforced our view that a recovery in domestic demand remains elusive. Fixed asset investment weakened further, with the contraction widening to 7.2% y/y YTD, reflecting broad-based deep contraction across infrastructure, property and manufacturing investment. Retail sales growth missed expectations, and has remained stuck at 1% or below for five consecutive months, an unprecedented stretch outside the pandemic years, with household sentiment and income expectations hovering around record low levels. Despite disappointing domestic demand, we maintain our below-consensus 2026 GDP growth forecast of 4.5%, the lower end of the growth target range of 4.5-5%. This largely reflects: 1) China's GDP growth is production based; and 2) IP was reported significantly stronger than demand-side indicators. That said, risks remain tilted to the downside if additional fiscal support is delayed. Moreover, we expect growth to slow further, to 4%, in 2027, reflecting the structural headwinds discussed below. For some central banks that are facing inflationary pressures, Switzerland currently enjoys inflation well below its target. We doubt that it will even challenge to out hawk the market. Whilst there is an argument that the SNB will warn about the upside risks to inflation and potentially revise up its forecasts, we do not think this will include projections for a rate hike. More likely, we think the SNB will leverage on the FX rate by dropping some of the verbal rhetoric that has been evident in speeches and policy decisions. This has precedence: through the Russia-Ukraine war, the SNB dropped reference to CHF being excessively overvalued and whilst our metrics still point to a strong currency, this SNB will likely use this as a de facto tightening instrument. We do not think that dropping the reference to FX will be a positive for CHF. The backdrop remains conducive to vol adjusted carry trades and the emergence of the BoJ from ultra low rates means CHF has become the natural funding currency in G10. Any bounce on dropping of the FX language should be used as an opportunity to sell CHF.

records.text: PI in the short term. However, in the longer term, inflation is a monetary phenomenon – and here we think the SNB is well - positioned to achieve its price-stability mandate. Despite short-term fluctuations in exchange rates, Switzerland remains one of the safest harbours. Compared to other central banks, the SNB does not need to counteract loose fiscal policies : Gross government debt is low relative to GDP and the country is running fiscal surpluses. Even the share of unfunded implicit pension liabilities is lower than in many other European countries. Separately, the SNB’s very large foreign asset holdings can to some extent act as an automatic stabiliser: When the CHF depreciates against other currencies , these holdings tend to become more valuable, thereby strengthening the backing behind the outstanding francs and making it easier for the SNB to drain excess francs from circulation if needed . Thus, inflation expectations should remain anchored within the target range, in our view, restraining potential second-round effects for inflation. The main reason why, contrary to our base case, the SNB may want to lift its policy rate next year, would be to limit the spread between its rate a nd those elsewhere. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 13 3Q GDP tracking raised ½ point to 2.5% We raised our 3Q GDP tracking by 0.5 pct pt to 2.5% from 2.0%. Strong August retail sales (and little revision to prior months) raised our estimate of 3Q real consumer spending growth by 0.8 pct pt to almost 3%. We allowed for somewhat slower inventory re-stocking than we had, which blunted some of the boost to GDP, but the effect was still a 0.4 pct increased from our prior GDP tracking. Another 0.1 pct pt boost to our estimate came from a housing starts report that was, on net, slightly stronger than we had allowed for. For a second quarter in a row, it appears that demand is running faster than output. While we estimate 3Q GDP rises at a 2.5% q/q annual rate, we estimate private final domestic final purchases (PDFP) rises at a 3.7% pace, with another quarter of booming business investment plus the 2.9% consumption growth. In 2Q, GDP rose 1.5% but PDFP rose 4.2%. The Atlanta Fed's estimate rose from 4.7% to 5.1%. Its faster pace mostly reflects two categories. Services consumption, at 4.6% growth, is a point and a half higher than ours, contributing an extra 0.7 pct pt to GDP growth. And the Atlanta Fed also is estimating that inventories add 2.0 pct pts to growth in 3Q, 1.7 pct pt more than we estimate. The New York Fed nowcast was unaltered at 2.3%. records.text: Borrower performance remains robust despite modest home price declines Despite home prices trending modestly lower, borrower on-time payment performance has remained resilient across various loan types—Conventional (i.e., Fannie and Freddie) loans, loans that are made to high credit quality borrowers but are underwritten using non-standard income/employment documentation (i.e., non-QM loans), or loans to weaker credit quality borrowers (such as FHA loans, Exhibit 9). This is largely a function of the large amounts of remaining home equity, following several years of above-average HPA, and a relatively healthy economy. New mortgages also have sufficient equity cushion in them, with the average loan amount to home value (LTV) ratio for Florida mortgages originated in 2025 at 83%. As of Q1 2026, only 1.9% of all mortgaged properties nationwide and just 1.2% of properties in the Miami metro area were underwater. While market participants are keenly monitoring delinquency rates in Florida and Texas, the continued benign delinquency rates have provided sufficient comfort to investors to buy non-investment grade tranches of recently issued non-QM deals despite the tranches trading near their tightest levels since the COVID housing boom. 18 September 2026 <#> Goldman Sachs Housing and Mortgage Monitor For the exclusive use of CAYLA.BUETTNER@BLUECRESTCAPITAL.COM 7595159db82544668b3260609400172c

records.text: ar-25 Dec-25 Consumer Income Confidence Index Quarterly Export YoY%-RS Source: CEIC, Morgan Stanley Research The US post-GFC experience shows how private-sector deleveraging can be offset by public-sector releveraging. US households repaired their balance sheets through debt repayment, defaults, and reduced borrowing, while parts of the corporate and financial sectors also reduced leverage. The public sector moved in the opposite direction. Federal government debt rose from roughly 64% of GDP in 2Q08 to 93% by 1Q11, and subsequently to around 110% following the pandemic. At the same time, the Federal Reserve adopted quantitative easing and maintained a low-yield environment for an extended period. Together, fiscal and monetary support underpinned nominal income growth, reduced real debt burdens, and ultimately helped stabilize house prices. The household deleveraging cycle ended once asset and income reflation replaced liability contraction as the primary adjustment mechanism. As house prices and employment recovered, stronger household wealth and disposable income supported a re-acceleration in borrowing without worsening debt-to-asset ratios. Even with active public balance-sheet expansion, US households required five years to deleverage. Despite a substantial policy offset, including a 29 percentage-point increase in federal debt in less than three years and large-scale QE, US household deleveraging persisted for roughly five years before debt growth resumed. Current crisis favors LNG supply diversification — into US LNG. While LNG buyers have not written off Qatar as a long-term supplier, there is growing interest in supply diversification at the margin, with the US as the likely winner of long-term contracts as a result. Client conversations suggest that this diversification push is not yet fully realized, with additional contract announcements likely going forward. That said, when it comes to European import contracts, both LNG importers and exporters expressed concern regarding the EU methane regulation, which requires EU importers of LNG to comply with the measurement, reporting and verification of methane leaks and emissions originating from overseas LNG producers. From Jan 1st, 2027, this will be required for all EU import contracts signed on or after August 2024. Although potential penalties for lack of compliance have been delayed by three years to 2030, market participants have expressed that the lack of clarity in the regulation and uncertainty as to which contract party should bear the burden of compliance have effectively kept some European buyers from signing such long-term LNG import contracts. records.text: Potential property tax reduction in Florida can boost home prices In November, voters in Florida are set to vote on a Constitutional amendment that proposes to lower property taxes for homeowners (primary residence) by exempting a larger portion of their assessment value from certain taxes, among other changes. Specifically, if approved, the amendment would increase the dollar amount of the home’s tax assessment value that is exempt from non-school property taxes from $25k currently to $150k in 2027 and $250k in 2028. The tax exemption would primarily apply to current resident homeowners. New Florida residents would retain the existing lower exemption until they meet a 5-year minimum residency requirement. Voters will decide on this Constitutional amendment during the November 3, 2026 elections. The amendment requires approval by at least 60% of voters. The probability of the proposed amendment passing has climbed to just over 50% on Polymarket recently. Several studies have found a negative relationship between property tax rates and housing prices, via what is known as the standard capitalization theory. This theory states that when the burden of owning a home declines (such as through lower property taxes), home buyers would be willing to pay the net present value of the decline in the housing burden and therefore should boost home prices immediately. For Issue 24, which redeems against December 2028 CPI, the corresponding effect is -48bp over 2.48 years. Issue 25 redeems against December 2029 CPI and therefore faces no redemption-index impact if the tax rate reverts in April 2029 as legislated; only coupons paid during the lower-indexation period are marginally affected. The same applies to Issue 26 and later bonds. A fairly valued BEI curve should therefore exhibit a two-bond trough, with Issues 23 and 24 trading roughly 80bp and 50bp below adjacent bonds, respectively, while Issues 22 and 25 sit outside it. Nonfuel and capital goods drove import prices in August Import prices rose 0.7% in August, following an upwardly revised -0.3% decline in July. The increase was driven by nonfuel prices, rather than energy. Fuel import prices edged down -0.1% in August, while petroleum goods prices rose just 0.1%. Nonpetroleum import prices increased 0.8% in August, accelerating from a 0.3% gain in July, with higher prices for nonfuel industrial supplies and materials, capital goods, and consumer goods contributing to the increase. Headline import prices rose 7.0% in the 12 months ending in August, up from 6.1% in July and the largest annual increase since August 2022. Nonpetroleum import prices rose 5.5% over the same period, accelerating from 4.6% in July and 4.4% in June. Capital goods import prices rose 0.9% in August, broadly maintaining July's upwardly revised 1.0% pace and following a 0.4% increase in June. The August increase was driven by computers, peripherals and semiconductors, industrial and service machinery, and telecommunications equipment. Over the last 12 months, capital goods import prices were up 7.3%, with nonelectrical machinery prices rising 9.0%. records.text: M Idea 8 Euro Area Rates Strategy: Modest Pressure Luca Salford, Maria Chiara Russo, Jasper Knyphausen If confirmed, a return to a 2% minimum reserve requirement (MRR) for euro area banks should have a modest and uneven tightening effect in money market conditions. With regards to mandatory reserves, the ECB has been tweaking its framework along two dimensions over the years: 1) the MRR ratio, and 2) remuneration of mandatory reserves and excess liquidity ( Exhibit 9 ). A return to a 2% ratio would be a realignment to the pre- sovereign crisis era. However, at the time, remuneration was at the MRO rate vs zero now, so this would be a net tightening for banks compared to pre-crisis, following years of very generous policies that skewed heavily in the opposite direction. An increase in minimum reserve requirements would automatically reduce excess liquidity, meaning money market rates would come under increasing pressure earlier. It would also bring forward the need for banks to obtain liquidity through ECB operations, which are currently being used only to a limited extent (Exhibit 10 ). records.text: Also this week Japan trade and Saudi pipeline shutdown – Japan’s trade balance showed a deficit in August due mainly to higher crude imports; the Saudi pipeline shutdown impacts heavily on Japan given that a fourth of its crude imports recently came from the Red Sea; near term, ample inventories should contain supply risks, but price risk remains: Japan’s August trade balance recorded a fourth consecutive monthly deficit as imports outpaced exports. Exports rose 19.3% y/y to JPY10.0trn, led by semiconductors and electronic components, automobiles (rebound to US after previous year’s tariff-induced price decline, increased exports to EU/ASEAN) and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, while imports increased 28.0% to JPY11.2trn. Crude oil was the main import driver, rising 58.7% y/y. Although August import prices eased on lower benchmark prices and Saudi premiums, international crude prices have since rebounded, with Dubai crude exceeding USD120/bbl. The shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline poses a significant risk because Red Sea- origin crude accounted for around one-quarter of Japan’s arrivals in July, including cargoes routed through Malaysia. Red Sea shipments have already largely ceased, and Japan plans to bridge September supply with inventories until rerouted (Suez/Cape of Good Hope) tankers arrive in October. The rate hike was decided, but its logic remains questionable The BoJ decided at its MPM today to raise its policy rate by 0.25 percentage points to 1.25%, a move widely anticipated by the market. However, board members Asada and Sato voted against the decision. Given that only member Asada had dissented at the June rate hike, the addition of another dissenter is a modest surprise. We share the view expressed in member Sato's reason for dissent: "current economic and price developments did not appear to have substantially accelerated compared to before." Indeed, the content of the statement released today is largely unchanged from the July Outlook Report, making it difficult to find a clear rationale for why the BoJ chose to hike rates in September rather than in July. In other words, this could be interpreted to suggest that the bar for back-to-back rate hikes is high at this point. If one were to pinpoint a change from the July meeting, it would be the reference to the high growth in Japan's producer price index (PPI). This suggests a recognition that upstream price pressures remain persistent and that the risk of this feeding through to the CPI is growing as firms become more willing to pass on costs. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 18 Sep 2026 05:47:56 ET │ 10 pages Japan Economics August nationwide CPI: Way station on the road back to 2%+ inflation again CITI'S TAKE The August nationwide core CPI (ex-fresh food) rose 1.7% YoY, down from +1.8% YoY in July and undershooting the market consensus. Food inflation continued to moderate amid declining rice prices, and energy’s contribution turned negative as the government reintroduced electricity and gas subsidies. These developments pushed core CPI down. Going forward, however, we expect higher oil prices due to the escalation of the Middle East situation to feed through to CPI with a lag, and core CPI looks likely to rise towards 3% again into early next year. While government subsidies are expected to offset the impact of rising oil prices to some extent during August-October, we expect core CPI to rise above 2% again in September, followed by a further acceleration from November and beyond. That said, this is well within the BoJ’s range of assumptions and thus should have a limited monetary policy impact, in our view. This risk was a key theme running through the minutes' individual paragraphs, where committee members gave explicit, conditional guidance. Governor Bailey noted, 'If the conflict in the Middle East persists for an extended period, as appears to be the case, and the risk of second-round effects emerging increases, it is likely that policy may have to tighten' . This week's August CPI data reflected the deterioration. Headline CPI accelerated to 3.1% y/y in August, driven by increased pump prices, with core inflation standing at 2.6% y/y, in line with our expectations. We raise our annual headline forecast 0.1pp, to 3.1%, in 2026 and 0.5pp, to 3.0%, in 2027. Although we still believe slack in the labour market and restrictive financial conditions will limit broader pass-through, we have adjusted our core inflation outlook 0.1-0.2pp higher at the peak in 2027. In view of these developments, our baseline is now for the MPC to raise the Bank Rate 25bp at its November meeting and, subject to continuation of the Middle East conflict, a further 25bp in February. When hiking to 2.50% in September, the ECB said inflation is expected to be “well above target for an extended period”. Around PLN40bn of upside risk to net issuance: We think the ministry will end up issuing around PLN40bn more than currently assumed. Growth in the cash balance is always assumed to be flat, but it has grown by an average of PLN40bn over the past five years, as the ministry targets a cash-to- expenditure ratio of between 25–35%. POLGB net issuance also tends to be revised up as the year progresses (Figure 5), driven by higher cash balances and deficit targets. We see the PLN164bn of net POLGB issuance for 2027 as a floor rather than a base case. Some relief could come from higher retail bond issuance, currently assumed flat, or stronger SAFE take-up. Still, with other domestic issuance (bills, linkers, FRNs) already running quite elevated, we expect any financing shortfall to spill over into higher POLGB issuance. What we are increasingly learning is that he is not like his predecessors. He took another step revealing his framework for implementing monetary policy in the press conference this week. The observations from Jackson Hole peppered the exchanges in the press conference, but if anything this week, he staked out an even more hawkish reaction function, how he maps the existing information into a setting for monetary policy. Framing Chairman Warsh's FOMC, past templates may no longer apply. This increasingly looks like a new regime, and a bigger break from the past than appreciated. What we are learning is that he is unlike any of his predecessors. His framework appears significantly less rooted in economic measurement details and significantly more reflective of market narratives. No Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve has emphasized considering the signals from financial markets as an input into monetary policy decisions as strongly as Chairman Warsh. Certainly, financial conditions matter for central banks. However, most Chairs see their end goals and seek to set policy and communications so that financial conditions are consistent with what the FOMC thinks will attain the goals of price stability and full employment. In contrast, Swiss consumer prices react much more slowly to higher international benchmark prices for natural gas . Besides petroleum products, household electricity is the most important subcomponent of energy prices in the Swiss CPI .1 However, these electricity tariffs generally only adjust once a year in January and suppliers need to report their prices for the year ahead by the end of August. Due to this, we know already that the median electricity tariff for a household with a standard consumption pattern will actually decline a little in 2027 compared to 2026. Thus, it will take until January 2028 before household electricity prices will push up CPI inflation – and even then, the headline rate will likely remain consistent with the SNB’s price stability target. Individual price changes , including prominently for energy products, can drive movements in the overall CPI in the short term. records.text: 21 September 2026 Global Economics Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. Page 10 United Kingdom Growth: The UK growth story continues to surprise forecasters. Q2 -26 GDP growth expanded by 0.4% q -o-q. Household spending so far this year is running at 0.9.% growth. Business investment is running closer to 2.5% growth. On an annualised basis, the UK economy is tracking at an impressive 2.4% run rate. The good news is that several capex cycles will likely keep UK GDP on an uptrend. AI spending is evident in the national accounts with the ICT sector alone expanding by 6.5% this year. Defence spending is also adding to momentum. And the government's industrial strategy is also running at full speed with public sector investment up over 10% in the last three quarters. The UK growth story won't go uninterrupted, however. A real income shock is in motion already. Tensions in the Middle East are poised to push inflation higher. Hiring plans remain flat to weak. And wage growth remains tempered. A course correction - as we've been warning all year - remains likely in the coming months. This shouldn't stop momentum from growing. We still see the UK's growth outperformance continuing. We have raised our Q3 -26 growth forecast to 0.5% q-o-q, while leaving Q4-26 unchanged at 0.1% q-o-q. This would see 2026 annual GDP grow by 1.3% - up 0.2pp from our previous projections. Fed review: Hike first, ask questions later As expected, the Fed hiked by 25bp at the Sep meeting, with a strongly hawkish message. The statement dropped language linking inflation to supply shocks (I.e., no more excuses), while the SEP showed stronger growth, higher inflation and a lower u- rate despite two hikes this year. Chair Warsh reinforced the message, making it clear that the job is not done. (see: US Watch: Sep FOMC review). Data review: Retail sales support booming nominal growth Aug retail sales surprised strongly to the upside, with ex-autos and control group sales both up 1.4% m/m. The strength was led by nonstore retailers, reflecting normalization after the shift in Prime Day from Jul to Jun. But the Aug gains were broad based, including a 1.2% rise in food services. Combined with positive revisions, the report led us to raise our 3Q PCE tracking estimate from 2.6% q/q saar to 3.4%. Bottom line: the nominal economy is booming, giving a monetarist like Warsh little reason to stop hiking. 18 September 2026 Economics United States US Economics BofAS Aditya Bhave US Economist BofAS +1 646 855 9929 aditya.bhave@bofa.com Stephen Juneau US Economist BofAS +1 202 442 7429 stephen.juneau@bofa.com Shruti Mishra

records.text: M Idea 6 Japan Macro Strategy: Market Pricing Has Gone Too Far Koichi Sugisaki, Hiromu Uezato, Japan Macro Strategy JPY Rates: Terminal-Rate Pricing Could Move Lower The BoJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% at the September meeting, as widely expected, but several aspects of the outcome looked dovish relative to market expectations. Ahead of the meeting, the dominant market view was that the BoJ needed to accelerate tightening to arrest JPY weakness. Immediately before the decision, markets priced one hike every three months and a terminal rate close to 2.25% (see Exhibit 4 ). As we noted in “Sep MPM Preview: BoJ Set to Raise Rates to 1.25%”, the bar for satisfying these market expectations was high. Three aspects of the statement may have looked particularly dovish: • Policy Board members Asada and Sato opposed the hike. • No member proposed a 50bp hike. • The statement contained no language pointing to a faster hiking pace, such as greater emphasis on upside inflation risks. Several points from Governor Ueda’s press conference may also have looked dovish relative to market expectation: • While Ueda did not rule out back-to-back hikes or a 50bp move, he suggested that such steps would be warranted only if underlying inflation faced a significant risk of exceeding 2%, or had already done so, as in the US and Europe in 2022. Economic activity and the labor market have both showed signs of firming since the July meeting, without material progress on inflation, and amid a more hostile geopolitical environment. There were interesting bits in the Fed’s communication. The statement and press conference were hawkish, reinforcing the price stability side of the mandate, and pointing to easy financial conditions in a decision to remove accommodation. The SEP was also hawkish, showing stronger growth, higher inflation, and a lower unemployment rate despite showing rate hikes. The market is pricing Fed hikes to perfection The market reaction was a clear bear flattening of the curve with rates selling off across all tenors. After the move, the markets are pricing around 100bp of hikes for the cycle. Even for us, who have long stressed the need for Fed hikes in the US, it is more than our 75bp forecast for the cycle, which is among the most hawkish on the Street. There are risks of further hikes, but the bar for Warsh to out-hawk the market appears high now. With the RBI announcing OMO sales recently, to reduce surplus liquidity on a durable basis, we believe the next natural step would be a 25bps hike in October, followed by another 25bps in December, before pausing briefly in February. Given the growth and inflation trajectory, we don’t think 50bps of hikes will be enough to establish sufficiently positive real rates to attract capital inflows and protect financial stability. If the Fed hikes 75bps in this cycle, India’s cycle should be at least 100bps, in our view. The RBI is unlikely to change the current neutral monetary policy stance already in October, but eventually it may change this to “restrictive” or “calibrated tightening” or “withdrawal of accommodation”, once the RBI has a better idea of how far the hiking cycle is likely to go. records.text: 3. Clients’ view: LNG demand destruction mainly expected in Asia, but uncertainty is high. Most market participants agree with our view that, if further LNG demand destruction is needed this winter, it’s likely to take place in Asia, not Europe. A few LNG buyers and sellers estimate $28-$30/mmBtu (85-90 EUR/MWh) as an important JKM price threshold for industrial demand destruction in India in particular, where LNG demand has been surprisingly resilient this summer2. That said, clients expressed concern that this price-driven demand destruction process might happen too slowly, especially if Asia governments intervene to help subsidize natural gas demand, which could take global LNG prices even higher. Several clients also raised the possibility of potential gas demand destruction from gas switching into oil products. Our take: The European energy crisis of 2022 has already destroyed significant European natural gas demand that has never come back3, suggesting it would take much higher gas prices to further dent local gas demand. With Europe typically driving 30% of global LNG demand, and Asia, more than 60%, this leaves the bulk of the demand adjustment to take place in Asia, in our view. We expect most of the gas demand destruction to take place in the industrial sector, which consumes a large amount of natural gas (Exhibit 4), well above the 30 mtpa of demand destruction we estimate would be needed under a low winter LNG supply scenario to help Europe manage its gas inventor

China’s economic planning system centers on the GDP growth target, which helps coordinate resources across ministries and different levels of government. Shifting to other targets, such as inflation or employment, would face various implementation challenges. At the same time, pressure to reach the growth target each year often leads to accelerated infrastructure investment, which is under policymakers’ control and can translate into GDP quickly. So we don’t think rates will reach the peak of 4.75% (unless things materially worsen), which the optimal policy path under the adverse scenario points to and which markets are pricing. QT decision adds more predictability to the QT process The MPC published a multi-year plan for its QT decision. It decided to reduce the stock of UK gilts held for monetary policy purposes to zero through a multi-year plan, such that the remaining stock is unwound at an annual average pace of £46bn by Sept. 2034, through annual sales of £20bn alongside maturing gilts. They have also set a high hurdle to future changes to the unwind path (such as severe gilt market stress or if Bank Rate is insufficient to meet the inflation target). Overall, the BoE has doubled down on making QT operate in the background, rather than an active policy tool. At the same time, pausing of active sales for potentially the next six months and selling bonds directly to the government were taken as a positive signal for the gilt market ahead of the Autumn Budget.

We continue to track core PCE around 3.0-3.1%Q4/Q4. Factors influencing our inflation assessment last week: (↓) After comments from Governor Waller a few weeks ago mentioning “a few tenths” of downward PCE revisions from upcoming methodology changes, we were surprised to see Fed officials raise their core PCE forecasts for this year in the September SEP , with a median forecast of 3.4%Q4/Q4. With revisions, we are currently penciling in 3.04%Q4/Q4 core PCE. It appears most likely that Fed officials are not including PCE revisions in their SEP forecasts. In the press conference, Chair Warsh mentioned an expectation for 3.2%YoY core PCE in August. In contrast to the SEP , we think this forecast from the Fed staff likely does incorporate upcoming revisions. Our forecast for August core PCE of 0.29%MoM and 3.14%YoY (unchanged after import prices) seems very close to Warsh’s expectation and does incorporate revisions. Absent revisions, we would be forecasting about 0.25%MoM and 3.37%YoY core PCE in August. Energy costs kick in with a lag here. While longer duration bonds historically provided more convexity during recessions and ‘risk off’ periods, the potential for large declines in long-dated bond yields might be more limited in the next crisis, and near-term rates volatility could remain somewhat elevated. Our rates strategists see the largest potential for rates relief in the front end vs. forwards, pointing to positions in the belly of the yield curve – that said, those would offer less convexity. Rates receiver swaptions on shorter-dated rates can provide a more convex hedge for a recession, with central banks likely to remain very responsive. While our Momentum Tracker (MMI) still shows solid Q3 growth, the pace of expansion is slowing. Growth risks may rise if Middle East tensions persist. records.text: As we discussed in our recent structural piece on Norway, our analysis suggests relatively little need for additional monetary tightening from current levels, as we forecast inflation pressures to moderate and growth to remain close to potential (Exhibit 6, left). There are, however, several important caveats. First, the recent moves higher in energy prices and product spreads suggest intensifying upside risk for inflation and the policy rate outlook, with potentially higher global inflation and a more aggressive hiking cycle abroad pushing Norges Bank to tighten further. Second, Norges Bank’s recent reaction function, proxied via their “judgement” applied on top of the model-implied policy rate forecast, appears considerably more hawkish in 2026 than in the last 5 years, on average (Exhibit 6, right). While their recent communication has softened slightly, the outlook for inflation, still elevated wage growth and imported, rather than domestic, drivers of recent inflation underperformance suggest that underlying inflationary pressures in Norway have not changed materially over the last months. Our baseline therefore remains one of a hike at the September meeting to 4.5%, but this is a close call and could materialise at a later meeting this year, followed by gradual easing towards a terminal rate of 3.5% in 2028. records.text: Production outlook in Venezuela On the back of the Chevron and ENI announcements in Venezuela on September 2, we update our Top Projects modelling for Venezuela in this note. In addition, the US-Venezuela oil agreement signed by Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, and Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, on 2 September implies further upside to our current modelled numbers. The deal gave the US majority control of >65 bn bbl of Venezuelan reserves, granting the US government governance rights, economic ownership and guaranteed low-cost off-take from a new private Venezuelan oil champion poised to be the second-largest private oil company by reserves in the world. Under the agreement, Venezuelan interim authorities granted North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a privately held operator and the second-largest private Venezuelan oil producer, 100-year concessions on 17 oil fields holding c.65 bn bbl of proven reserves. In connection with this agreement, the US Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital was granted a 35% equity stake in NABEP’s parent, and the US Department of State secured the right to purchase 20% of NABEP’s off-take at production cost, with right of first refusal on the remaining 80%. NABEP has flagged intent to invest up to $100bn over 25 years, with output routed through US refineries. As a result, we see Venezuelan crude reaching c.1.9 mboed by 2030 (+945 kboed vs 2025) and c.2.3 mboed by 2035 with upside to those numbers if more companies come on-strea

The combination of weak job prospects, elevated youth unemployment and shrinking hiring plans points to persistent labour market stress. • Manufacturing investment is becoming increasingly weak and bifurcated. Overall investment has been contracting since April, but beneath the surface, strategic industries continue to attract capital while traditional and labor-intensive sectors (eg, autos, ferrous and nonferrous metals) retrenched. High-tech investment rose 5.2% y/y YTD, led by information services (+23%), lithium-ion batteries (+21%), aerospace and aircraft equipment manufacturing (+15%) and semiconductors and electronic circuits (+12%). However, the high-tech sector remains too small to compensate for broad-based weakness in other sectors. As a result, manufacturing investment is likely to remain weak despite pockets of strength in high-tech industries. • Infrastructure investment has contracted at a double-digit pace for four straight months. The slowdown reflects more selective project approvals, a growing emphasis on investment quality and returns, and persistent caution among local governments constrained by debt burdens and tighter oversight. While some pickup is likely, we don't expect another infrastructure boom. The money market—the operations normalisation supports the front end The switch of the climate-response operations to a floating rate with a JPY50trn cap works on front-end rates through a channel separate from the pace of hikes. Once one-year fixed-rate funding with a balance of about JPY25trn becomes floating, the incentive to fund through the facility fades, demand for the T-bills pledged as collateral falls and funding shifts to the interbank and repo markets. That points to the end of the low, stable T-bill yields and to TONA and the uncollateralised call rate drifting higher relative to the policy rate. The 1y OIS has room to price this rise in funding costs on top of policy expectations, which gives the OIS 1s2s flattener (pay 1y, receive 2y) a support unrelated to policy expectations. For meeting-date OIS receivers, by contrast, a higher TONA is a small headwind, so the 1.49 stop on the December–January receiver should be judged on policy expectations after netting out that drift. The asymmetry the economics section describes—fast normalisation of funding facilities, slow hikes—translates on the front end of the curve into "the policy-rate cadence is slow, but the normalisation of funding costs comes first", which works to flatten the curve between one and two years. Orinoco crude has API gravity of 9.5–12, and sulfur content of 4%–5%, making it comparable to Canada’s oil sands bitumen (link). The Orinoco Belt’s heavy crude oil is extracted by horizontal multilateral wells (link). This technique is called cold heavy oil production (CHOPs). This is when sand is injected into a perforated hole, resulting channels allow crude oil to flow to the surface, either by itself or via secondary recovery techniques. For multilateral wells, OCTG requirements focus on high-performance connections, robust materials (like corrosion resistant alloys or CRAs), and connection testing protocols that simulate complex downhole conditions (pressure, temperature, high doglegs, mechanical loads, fatigue, and corrosion) to ensure well integrity, especially for production casing that supports multiple branches and stimulation cycles. We estimate Venezuela OCTG demand could reach 140-240kt by 2030; and $0.6-1bn market size. He noted that September's hike 'removed a dose of accommodation' , rather than bringing policy into restrictive territory. To us, Warsh's focus on the fact that financial conditions remain insufficiently restrictive implies that further tightening may be necessary to bring financial conditions into alignment with the committee's inflation objectives. We maintain our Fed call, with another 25bp rate hike in December and then maintaining this setting for most of 2027. We expect the FOMC to cut rates 25bp in December 2027, with inflation forecast to move closer to the 2% target. Given the hawkish surprise, we view the risks to our funds rate outlook as tilted to the upside. BoE holds, but signals future hikes Divided vote for hold, as expected A day after the Fed, the BoE's MPC voted by a majority of 6-3 to keep the Bank Rate on hold at 3.75%. This was expected. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 18 September 2026 5 For one, the rate hike alleviates concerns that Warsh is not politically independent. Additional increases would end that conversation for good. For another, by hiking at just his third meeting as Fed Chair, Warsh can absolve himself of the inflation problem, while also taking credit for any disinflation in coming months. We expect the BEA’s methodological revisions and the rolling off of tariff and Iran effects from y/y inflation to push the core PCE toward 2.5% by the middle of next year (Exhibit 2). None of this would be a function of rate hikes, but the optics would be favorable for Warsh because he took action and the previous regime did not. The irony is that the opportunity for these favorable optics only arose because core inflation rose very quickly at the start of the year and two factors beyond the Fed’s control sealed the deal for the September hike. First, oil prices ratcheted up significantly in the run-up to the meeting. And second, the Treasury’s buyback program backfired, contributing to the spike in yields that amplified concerns that the long end could de- anchor if the Fed’s credibility was called into question. Will rate hikes work? But let’s not forget the lesson of the parable: “We’ll see”. records.text: As has been the case over the past few years, the drivers of any rate increases are far more important than the absolute levels. Higher rates reflecting resilient growth are more easily digested by credit fundamentals. Higher base rates may support increased demand for floating rate credit, such as direct lending loans (within private credit) or broadly syndicated loans (either outright or as part of structured investments). That said, it is unlikely to be the key driver of investor demand, in our view, and will need to be accompanied by a supportive macroeconomic backdrop and compelling relative value. Framing the recent improvement in debt service costs, credit metrics Heading into the most recent rate hike from the Fed, floating rate borrowers in the broadly syndicated loan and private credit markets demonstrated an improvement in interest coverage metrics over the past several quarters. The cumulative 175bp of Fed rate cuts from September 2024 through December 2025 materialized through lower floating-rate borrowing costs—easing some of the fundamental pressure which occurred following the Fed’s 525bp rate hiking cycle from March 2022 through July 2023. For example, the weighted-average institutional rate for new USD leveraged loans fell to 6.5% in 2Q2026, from 9.3% in 3Q2023 (Exhibit 3). Page 13 China Growth: China’s economy remained K-shaped through July and August, and the rebound in domestic demand fell short of our expectations. Our model estimates that real GDP growth edged up only 0.1ppt to 4.2% YoY in August, still below the government’s 4.5 -5% target range. Industrial production accelerated, but services output slowed to 4.1% and retail sales dipped to 0.4%. Fixed asset investment remained weak at -10.5% YoY. We therefore lower our full-year 2026 GDP growth forecast by 0.1ppt to 4.6%, with Q3 and Q4 growth now forecast at 4.4% and 4.6%, respectively. External demand remains a strong growth engine. Exports and imports accelerated to 25% YoY and 28.2% YoY in August, respectively, with their July -August averages exceeding Q2 levels. AI -related products contributed 12ppt to export growth, while consumer goods and refined petroleum exports also strengthened. Inflation: Reflation regained momentum in August, providing relief after two consecutive months of sequential declines. Headline CPI rose 0.4% MoM, supported by higher fuel and gold prices, firmer services inflation, resilient AI - related demand and recovering pork prices. PPI increased 0.4% MoM, with improvement across 20 of 33 industries. Nevertheless, weak domestic deman d continues to weigh on most consumer goods, making the rebound potentially temporary. records.text: 37% in the last week of August, the CBT kept policy unchanged in September and highlighted upside risks to inflation. We continue to expect two 100bp rate cuts at the final MPC meetings of the year, on 22 October and 10 December, which would bring the policy rate down to 35% by YE26, compared with our YE26 inflation forecast of 30.0% y/y. While strong fiscal discipline and the sliding-scale fuel pricing mechanism continue to cushion the economy from higher energy costs, the current account deficit is widening. Over the final five months of the year, we expect an additional current account deficit of $18.2bn, bringing the full-year tally to $53.0bn. Using financing patterns from the corresponding period a year ago for FDI, portfolio flows, borrowing, deposits, financial derivatives, and net errors and omissions, we estimate that CBT gross reserves and net reserves excluding swaps could decline by around $26.2bn by YE26, to approximately $138bn and $15bn, respectively. Under this scenario, net reserves excluding swaps could fall into negative territory by Q1 27 if energy prices remain elevated. Likewise, if Brent crude averages around $100/bbl through the remainder of 2026 and throughout 2027, we believe the CBT would be inclined to keep its policy rate unchanged at 37.0% in 2026, with only limited room, around 200bp, for easing in 2027. We expect sequential growth to pick up in coming n months, supported by faster government bond issuance and increasing infrastructure investment. But that would still leave Q3 and Q4 real GDP growth at 4.4% yoy and full-year growth at 4.5%, the lower bound of the government’s 4.5-5.0% target. Annual growth targets help coordinate resources and support the long-term objective of “doubling income by 2035,” but they also push the government to lean on investment whenever growth slows, delaying rebalancing. The path of least resistance may be gradual RMB appreciation and more export-rebate cuts to manage large trade surpluses and rising trade tensions, alongside a gradual downgrade of the annual growth target—for example, from “4.5-5.0%” in 2026 to “around 4.5%” in 2027. records.text: Looking ahead, we, however, nudge our forecast higher and now see core inflation only slightly lower than the latest Norges Bank’s forecast from Q4 onwards (Exhibit 4, left). We also revise our headline inflation forecast up more notably, partly driven by an end of the fuel tax subsidy in September, and now see it peaking at 3.6%yoy in 2026Q4 (vs. 3.3%yoy previously). Besides, the latest Regional Network Survey (RNS) showed nominal wage growth expectations unchanged at 4.5% for this year, supporting the notion that underlying inflationary pressures in Norway remain broadly unchanged (Exhibit 4, right). As opposed to Sweden, activity in Norway has been broadly subdued so far this year, with an average sequential quarterly pace of GDP growth of 0.2% in H1, driven by two quarters of contracting private consumption. We, however, expect Q3 to show a stronger pace of growth, with the monthly nowcast, mapping our monthly CAI into GDP , suggesting an expansion of 0.5%qoq, mildly supported by higher energy prices (Exhibit 5, left). We thus expect annual GDP growth of 1.1% this year, close to consensus (1.0%) and Norges Bank’s (0.9%) forecast, but see downside risk to our 2027 forecast, driven by stronger global growth and domestic consumption (Exhibit 5, right). Economic activity was described as solid, with resilient consumer spending, despite elevated uncertainty; strong productivity growth; robust investment; and a stable labour market, with unemployment little changed. The statement avoided offering any guidance on future policy moves, consistent with Chair Warsh's strong aversion toward forward guidance and in line with the previous two statements. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 11 The effective tariff rate, tariff receipts, and refunds Tariffs averaged 6.7% over May-July, and we expect that it will rise to near 10% USTR's final forced-labor Section 301 action was broadly in line with our expectations. Effective July 24, the agency imposed additional tariffs on imports from 60 economies, setting a 10% duty on economies that have adopted, partially adopted, or committed to adopt a forced-labor import prohibition and a 12.5% duty on most others. The final action also preserves several key carve-outs, including goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs, USMCA-compliant imports, and a range of general and country-specific product exemptions. Overall, both the tariff structure and the principal exemptions closely resemble the proposal, reinforcing our expectation that Section 301 would serve as the broad country-level tariff floor. We continue to expect that the statutory effective tariff rate will converge toward ~10% by year-end. In the July 2026 data, the effective tariff rate is estimated at ~6.5%. Over the past three months of detailed trade data (May, June and July), the tariff rate has averaged 6.7%. There has been a recent escalation of trade disputes with Canada, and section 338 tariffs have been applied on approximately $20bn of Canadian imports. records.text: Debt service costs are likely more relevant vs. business model pressures, in our view While interest rate considerations are a standard part of credit investors’ relative value calculus—as there is a direct impact on total returns, the widely-discussed ‘yield-based demand,’ and debt service costs—we sense that the tone of the focus has shifted in a more negative direction, especially as it relates to fundamental risks facing floating rate borrowers. There are two key channels of fundamental impact for this cohort, in our view. First is on the debt service cost, as floating rate borrowers will experience a headwind in the form of higher interest costs immediately, while the fixed rate borrowers will experience higher interest costs only if/when they refinance their lower-coupon debt. Second is the impact on specific business models. The increase in interest rates may weigh on consumer demand in interest rate sensitive areas of the economy, where financing is a key ingredient to purchases, such as real estate, autos, and areas of home improvement (high-priced appliances, for example). The pressure on discretionary income may be especially visible at the lower end of the income spectrum, which spends a larger share of their budget on energy costs. That said, our US economists have noted that household balance sheets are strong, and the net worth-to-disposable personal income ratio is still near its all-time high—somewhat tempering this risk. However, leading figures across the Conservative camp remain aligned on the need for structural reforms, and the party will keep pushing for them under any leadership. Moreover, any plausible successor from the CDU/CSU would likely remain committed to the new fiscal policy paradigm established by Merz last spring. There has been little substantive criticism within the CDU/CSU of the government’s fiscal stance. While the reform of the debt brake might have damaged the Chancellor’s standing among parts of the electorate, criticism from within the party has focused primarily on communication rather than policy. records.text: ise rates either. If the Fed were to stay on hold in the face of a rising r*, it would implicitly be easing. That wouldn’t be a desirable outcome with the labor market at full employment and inflation overshooting the target. Warsh has a great opportunity to push underlying inflation back to target Finally, some analysts are of the view that the Fed didn’t need to hike because underlying inflation is already close to 2%, and the overshoot is almost entirely due to supply disruptions that will roll off the y/y rate in short order. Our view is that underlying inflation has been stuck around 2.5% for several quarters because policy isn’t tight enough to push it back to 2% (Exhibit 1). Moreover, we think the resilience of the economy changes the Fed’s risk/reward calculus. On the one hand, it presents Warsh with an opportunity to make a stronger push to get inflation all the way back to target, without risking a recession, than Powell’s Fed was willing or able to do. This seems to be a stroke of good fortune, and we think Warsh is doing the right thing by seizing the moment. On the other hand, robust nominal growth increases the risk that if the Fed doesn’t tighten, demand-driven inflation could pick up as the supply shocks fade.

LLC Global Markets Daily: Timing It Right — When to Sell Interest Rates Vol 18 September 2026 | 4:16AM EDT The rise in yields year to date has so far come alongside relatively contained n realized volatility across much of the curve. That said, there have been pockets of higher implied volatility over the year, though these have generally been followed by vol under-delivering what was priced. Implied volatility typically embeds a premium over realized volatility that on n average results in positive returns to systematic vol selling. Year to date, such strategies generated monthly returns of around 1%, above the recent average. However, vol shocks pose risks, and some environments are more supportive for harvesting vol premium than others. We use different models to help identify how favorable conditions are for vol n selling. Specifically, we consider the level of implied volatility relative to macro fundamentals, changes in the pricing of growth and policy factors across a suite of macro assets, and implied vol versus what is predicted by a purely statistical framework. Using the forecasting accuracy of the different models as weights, we can then extract an aggregate signal about expected future returns to short-vol strategies across major tenors. records.text: US Economics Weekly18 September 2026 ab 11 FOMC recap: a hike with signs for more The FOMC voted 12-0 to raise the target range for the federal funds rate 0.25 pp to 3.75% to 4.00%. Chairman Warsh's press conference suggested at least one more rate hike was likely. The Summary of Economic Projections signalled that too. The median assumptions of appropriate policy revised higher. The so-called dot plot showed a median participant assumes another 0.25 pp rate hike this year will be appropriate, and that it would be appropriate to maintain that 4.1% midpoint of the target range throughout 2027. No cuts until 2028, and even by the end of 2029, the target range for the federal funds was still 3.50% to 3.75%, despite having returned inflation to 2.0%. The dot plot suggested a widespread rethinking of how restrictive policy would need to be in order to return inflation to 2.0% and keep it there. The FOMC's dot plot revealed a Committee acting like the neutral rate might be over 3.5%. Chairman Warsh's press conference comments laid out a clearer retrospective of the decisions and communications since he arrived, and built upon the principles at Jackson Hole. He said more than once that financial conditions are not restrictive. He said that the 0.25 pp rate hike removed only "a dose of accommodation" more than once. records.text: 18 Europe Economic Weekly | 18 September 2026 2027 budget negotiations and election campaign are ongoing We still see a path for a 2027 budget to be passed before year-end. We don’t expect a smooth process but expect presidential election candidates to focus on their promises of a post-election rewrite of the budget, rather than present a vehement objection to the government’s plan. We also acknowledge the high uncertainty over 2027 macro forecasts in the Euro area, especially in France. An extreme outcome in the presidential election, and the likely subsequent parliamentary election, could result in a significant shift from the status quo in both French and EU policymaking, we think. We are worried about France, but some perspective is still needed Of course, idiosyncratic French risks abound and ultimately deficit correction will be needed. Pointing a finger at Euro area peers won’t make the French challenge disappear. But we still think a little bit of perspective is warranted: Starting points matter. In our view, the popular “glass half full” Italian narrative stands in too stark contrast with the French “glass rather empty” one. France’s debt ratios are still well below Italy’s (116% vs 137% in 2025), debt servicing costs are lower (2% vs 3.9% of GDP in 2025). This is above the 1.1% lower-end estimate of the neutral rate from the Goy-Iwasaki model, one of several models referenced by the BoJ. records.text: Latin America Outlook Far from over The shocks have left Latin America relatively resilient, supported by energy availability, growth and fuel subsidies. But trade uncertainty, the Iran conflict, El Niño, higher long- term yields and a hawkish Fed add complexity to fiscal and monetary policy decisions. The shocks are far from over. Shocks, but resilience. Latin America has managed to come through relatively unscathed after a series of consecutive shocks, including a more protectionist US trade policy and, more recently, the conflict with Iran. In our view, three important issues that have explained this resilience are: (1) the region has not faced physical scarcity of oil or fuels, partly because more countries have developed or enhanced either oil extraction capabilities or refining infrastructure, particularly Brazil and Argentina; (2) the crisis in the Middle East caught Latin America in a positive growth momentum; and (3) both (1) and (2) have allowed governments in many countries to fully or at least partially subsidize fuel prices, keeping inflation levels relatively low and allowing consumers to keep their consumption patterns mostly unchanged. Shocks are far from over. Not only does uncertainty surrounding US trade policy appear likely to persist, but the conflict in Iran also seems likely to drag on. And now, El Niño, higher yields at the long end of the curve stemming from growing strains in the US fixed income market, and a more hawkish Fed have entered the picture

In 2007 and 2008 then Governor Warsh seemed sympathetic to arguments by FOMC participants like Charles Plosser and Richard Fisher, who supported higher rates at the time, worried that rising oil prices would prove more inflationary despite weakening economic conditions. Because oil prices do not keep rising forever, they eventually level off, and the growth in prices (inflation) is zero. Then, if monetary policy reacts to the initial shock, the policy setting would then be offsides after the shock ends; hence the arguments to "look through" supply shocks. Chairman Warsh's criticism of the Fed's handling of 2020-2022 likely added to his opposition to "look through." Instead, monetary policy should worry about supply shocks and in the face of them, push back to keep inflation at target. M Idea 10 Financial conditions: Into a new hiking cycle Following the 25bp rate hike in September and the shift into an "oil risk premium" baseline, we reset our financial conditions index to September 15 2026, the day prior to the September FOMC meeting, to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions in this new hiking cycle. As of the September 17 market close, financial conditions were slightly easier than they were before the September FOMC meeting. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since the day before the September FOMC meeting, the easing in financial conditions has been equivalent to about an 8bp cut in the federal funds rate. Financial conditions initially tightened by 6bps on the day of the FOMC meeting, but eased by 14bps the following day, driven primarily by a lower 10-year Treasury yield and stronger equity returns. records.text: A decisive move to rebalance the domestic economy may involve either expanding fiscal spending substantially to boost consumption or drastically shifting fiscal spending from investment to consumption. Policymakers are reluctant to do the former because of debt sustainability concerns, given that China’s augmented fiscal deficit has run in double digits as a share of GDP every year since 2015. They are also reluctant to do the latter because of growth target concerns, as the GDP impact of reducing investment would be immediate, whereas the benefits of strengthening the social safety net would come much later. The path of least resistance may be to gradually lower the annual growth target, for example from 4.5-5.0% in 2026 to around 4.5% in 2027. More signals on next year’s growth target should emerge as the December Politburo meeting and Central Economic Work Conference approach later this year. records.text: M Idea 2 energy-driven inflation pressures strengthens the case for a firmer dollar. Over recent months, rising energy prices supported the euro because investors assumed the ECB would respond more aggressively than the Fed. That perceived asymmetry may now be changing. If investors conclude that both central banks are prepared to lean against energy-related inflation risks, higher energy prices become less euro- supportive and increasingly dollar-supportive. Our FX strategists therefore continue to favor dollar strength, particularly against the yen. Europe faces a similar inflation challenge, though through a different transmission channel. The renewed rise in natural gas and energy prices has led our economists to revise their inflation outlook materially higher and to add another ECB rate hike in December, followed by a much shallower easing cycle in 2027. Importantly, however, energy prices alone do not explain the change in outlook. Euro area activity has proven more resilient than anticipated, reducing concerns that modest additional tightening would derail growth. As a result, the ECB is increasingly focused on preventing higher energy costs from feeding into broader inflation dynamics, even as policy rates move further into restrictive territory. Exhibit 2: We see materially higher inflation in the Euro area given higher energy prices, and now expect another hike in December, a lengthier hold and shallower easing in 2027. Assessing the persistence of 2% inflation One indicator of underlying inflation that has recently attracted attention is the share of items recording inflation rates above 3%, which Federal Reserve Chair Warsh highlighted as a useful gauge of underlying inflation. When assessing whether Japan’s 2% inflation target is becoming firmly entrenched, it is important to evaluate not only the level and breadth of inflation, but also its persistence. To this end, we examine the share of CPI items whose year-on-year price increases have remained above 2% for at least 12 consecutive months. This measure provides insight into how the persistence, or “stickiness,” of inflation in Japan has evolved over time. Our findings suggest that the persistence of 2% inflation may be gradually strengthening. We continue to expect additional rate hikes in January and July after the September move As this meeting provided no concrete hints about future rate hikes, we stick to our base case that, following September, the BoJ will deliver additional hikes in January and July next year to a terminal rate of 1.75%. As noted above, Governor Ueda remarked on the need to carefully assess financial conditions. Today's August CPI came in below expectations. With sticky services inflation also stagnating at just over 1%, the likelihood of second-round effects remains low for now, suggesting little need to rush rate hikes to curb inflation. However, if renewed JPY depreciation pushes USDJPY well above 160 again, pressure from the US side could compel the BoJ to deliver further hikes.
