records.text: 4 US Economic Weekly | 18 September 2026 Why the Fed hiked into a supply shock? The first contention is that the Fed shouldn’t be hiking into a supply shock. When asked about this, Warsh said that the Fed’s job is to prevent the increase in commodity prices from broadening out. Here’s how we interpret that comment. The concern about hiking into a supply shock is that real growth might be already weakening, and the hikes would inflict even more pain on the economy. But the real economy has been stable of late, even as inflation has picked up. I.e., nominal growth has been booming. That’s what exacerbates the risk that the commodity shock could broaden out. From Warsh’s monetarist perspective, the growth rate of the nominal economy is a function of the velocity of money and the money supply. The response to robust nominal growth is to slow the velocity of money by hiking rates. Indeed, the data support the case for reining in nominal growth. Nominal spending is up 6.3% y/y. History suggests core PCE tends to overshoot 2% when nominal spending is running above 5% (Exhibit 3). The late 90s tech productivity boom was an exception, and AI-driven productivity could deliver a similar outcome. But until there is clear evidence of disinflation due to AI, the Fed has little choice but to tighten policy. However, a key theme is the widening divergence between nominal and real growth. Strong global AI demand is boost ing corporate earnings mostly through a price effect, lifting export prices and nominal GDP, while its contribution to real GDP will be limited by severe domestic supply constraints. Labor shortages and production backlogs for machinery are capping both export volume and capital investment growth, despite firm corporate plans. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 18 September 2026 11 points to a renewed tightening in corporate financing conditions since the start of the Iran conflict, with the worsening largely concentrated in price-related components, notably lending rates. In other words, the main challenge for corporates currently appears to be the rising cost of credit rather than an outright lack of access to financing. That said, SAFE survey evidence suggests that this pattern may not persist indefinitely. While firms on aggregate reported broadly unchanged availability of bank loans in 2Q26, the picture was markedly weaker for SMEs which continued to report a deterioration in credit availability and a widening financing gap (Exhibit 11). By contrast, large firms reported an improvement in access to bank credit. This divergence is important because tighter pricing conditions often translate into quantity restrictions with a lag, particularly for smaller and more bank-dependent firms. The deterioration in SMEs' perceptions of credit availability therefore suggests that the transmission of tighter financing conditions may already be underway, even if aggregate credit origination has remained relatively resilient so far. Put differently, the impact of recent tightening has so far been most visible through the price channel, but “quantity effects” may increasingly emerge in coming quarters through impaired access to credit, especially for SMEs. records.text: Path of Least Resistance The Gap Keeps Growing China’s August activity data showed a widening divergence between supply and demand, and between manufacturing output and household consumption. Industrial production growth accelerated from 4.5% yoy in July to 5.2% in August, while retail sales growth slowed from 0.6% yoy to 0.4%. Among major activity indicators, only export value and industrial production growth exceeded 5.0% yoy in August. By contrast, many domestic demand gauges continued to post large year-over-year declines (Exhibit 1). For exports, we can cross-check the data against trading partners’ reported imports from China. Such “mirror data” support strong Chinese export growth. For domestic demand, however, there are statistical reasons why official data may understate the true weakness. For example, in retail sales, large retailers above the designated size are surveyed comprehensively, whereas small retailers are sampled and estimated because of their large numbers and the difficulty of surveying every small retailer each month (see our latest edition of “Understanding China’s Economic Statistics” for more details). As a result, officially reported sales growth at small retailers tends to be smoother than that at large retailers and to hold up better during economic downturns. records.text: 6 Global Economic Weekly | 18 September 2026 Here’s how we interpret that comment. The concern about hiking into a supply shock is that real growth might be already weakening, and the hikes would inflict even more pain on the economy. But the real economy has been stable of late, even as inflation has picked up. I.e., nominal growth has been booming. That’s what exacerbates the risk that the commodity shock could broaden out. From Warsh’s monetarist perspective, the growth rate of the nominal economy is a function of the velocity of money and the money supply. The response to robust nominal growth is to slow the velocity of money by hiking rates. Indeed, the data support the case for reining in nominal growth. Nominal spending is up 6.3% y/y. History suggests core PCE tends to overshoot 2% when nominal spending is running above 5% (Exhibit 4). The late 90s tech productivity boom was an exception, and AI-driven productivity could deliver a similar outcome. But until there is clear evidence of disinflation due to AI, the Fed has little choice but to tighten policy. Especially given that i) today’s nominal spending numbers are even more impressive in the context of much slower population growth, and ii) globalization was also driving disinflation in the 90s, whereas now we are in a phase of inflationary deglobalization. records.text: Autodesk Problem: As extreme weather events become more frequent and severe, infrastructure and asset owners often lack visibility into asset conditions and vulnerabilities to proactively manage climate-related risks and plan long-term investments. Solution: Autodesk's digital twin solutions create digital representations of physical assets by integrating engineering designs, operational information and real-time data into a single platform. These tools enable infrastructure owners to monitor asset conditions, identify vulnerabilities, model the impacts of extreme weather, and optimise maintenance and investment decisions. Commercial Opportunity: Autodesk's digital twin solutions are used across transportation, water, buildings and other infrastructure assets. Demand is being supported by growing investment in infrastructure modernisation and increasing adoption of digital tools to improve asset resilience and manage climate-related risks. Business Implications: Management has positioned digital twins as a key long-term growth opportunity and is investing in the acquisition of companies to boost its offerings. The MaintainX acquisition is expected to advance Autodesk's strategy from static twins to dynamic and ultimately predictive digital twins. This strengthens Autodesk's exposure to a $40bn operations market across infrastructure, manufacturing, data centres and buildings, while increasing its role in resilience planning, predictive maintenance and climate-risk management.

We are also upgrading our previous risk scenario of a further rate hike to 1.75% in March 2027 to our new base case. Governor Ueda noted that, while the exchange rate is not itself the objective of monetary policy, policy rate increases by overseas central banks can affect Japanese inflation through various channels, including the exchange-rate channel, with yen depreciation clearly in mind. This suggests that the weight assigned to exchange-rate developments in the BoJ’s policy reaction function may have increased somewhat relative to the past. Our US economics team had previously expected the Fed to begin cutting rates in 2027. However, following consecutive revisions to its outlook on 14 and 17 September, it now expects further rate hikes in December 2026 and March 2027. records.text: Company case studies: Adaptation solutions in action Rockwool Problem: Rising wildfire risk, higher cooling demand and tighter building standards are increasing demand for resilient building materials that can improve fire safety, durability and energy efficiency. Solution: Rockwool provides hazard-resistant building materials made from non- combustible stone wool that enhances fire resilience, helps limit fire spread, and improves thermal performance during periods of extreme heat or cold. Its solutions also offer acoustic insulation and moisture management benefits, supporting more durable and resilient building envelopes. Commercial Opportunity: Rockwool's products are used across residential, commercial and institutional buildings (such as hospitals), with demand driven by both new construction and retrofit projects focused on improving fire safety and building resilience. The opportunity is supported by three structural drivers: tighter fire-safety regulations, rising cooling demand and accelerating retrofit activity aimed at improving building resilience. Business Implications: Rockwool illustrates how adaptation-linked regulation can become a structural growth driver. Management continues to report strong demand for non- combustible insulation, particularly in the US, while tighter European fire-safety standards are supporting share gains from flammable alternatives. records.text: Riksbank and Norges Bank Diverging Once More? Ahead of the Riksbank’s and Norges Bank’s September meetings, in this Daily we update the near-term outlook for Sweden and Norway, incorporating higher energy prices and recent activity and inflation data. We stick with our call that the Riksbank will stay on hold at the upcoming meeting, as the Board will need to see more evidence of broader and more persistent inflationary pressures before warranting earlier tightening. Norges Bank’s September meeting decision remains a very close call, as recent inflation surprises and broadly subdued activity point to less need for additional tightening beyond 4.25%. However, we maintain our call for a final 25bp hike to 4.5% at this week’s meeting, taking into account the hawkish bias in the reaction function and the fact that underlying inflationary pressures in Norway have not changed materially over the last months. Riksbank Will Stay on Hold in September At its last meeting in August, the Riksbank’s Executive Board left the policy rate unchanged at 1.75%, in line with our and consensus expectations. The communication appeared balanced, which, in the context of recent data surprises, sounded somewhat dovish. records.text: , a critical question was how Chair Warsh would frame the tightening cycle that lies ahead. We posited at least three possibilities. First, he could have argued that the hike was for risk management reasons. In this framing, the Fed’s modal economic outlook was mostly unchanged, but with upside risks to inflation intensifying and the labor market stable it made sense to take out insurance against stickier inflation. Second, Warsh could have characterized the rate increase as part of a process to undo the 75bps of rate cuts delivered last year, which have left the Fed overinsured against downside risks to the labor market (see “ Overinsured?”). Third, he could have argued that rate increases were intended to return policy to a sufficiently restrictive stance against a backdrop of a rising neutral rate. These options were neither mutually exclusive nor exhaustive. The first two options were more dovish framings in our view, as they would provide a concrete sense of the anticipated terminal rate from the tightening cycle. Risk management hikes suggest at most three hikes. Unwinding last year’s cuts frames the current hiking cycle as topping out at 75bps of rate increases. The third possibility was the most hawkish from a market perspective. It would leave expectations for the terminal rate open -ended, to be determined by the degree of tightening in financial conditions ultimately required to return inflation to target with sufficient speed. Super El Niño is likely emerging Current weather conditions suggest this El Niño could rank among the strongest on record. Pacific Ocean temperatures are already around 1.4°C above long-term averages, suggesting this may be among the most significant El Niño occurrences observed in recent decades. While no two El Niño events are the same, El Niño often means hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires. We do not find a material impact on headline inflation We measure the impact of El Niño on macroeconomic variables with the Vector Autoregression framework also used in Global Economic Viewpoint: El Niño risks are building. Our results indicate that El Niño may lower GDP, and while there may be some modest headline disinflationary pressure, we do not find any statistically significant effect on inflation overall. This likely reflects the fact that the GDP drag is concentrated in agriculture and trade-exposed sectors, while other parts of the economy provide an offsetting boost, such as construction which benefits from drier conditions. records.text: Japan Macro Watch18 September 2026 ab 5 Strong growth in household financial assets The Bank of Japan released its Q2 Flow of Funds Accounts statistics. Household financial assets rose 11.0% year-on-year to ¥2,519 trillion, maintaining a strong pace of growth. The increase was driven primarily by gains in equities and investment trusts amid continued strength in stock prices during Q2, with the 18 % gain in the Nikkei 225 average. Household holdings of equities and other risk assets surged 47.0% year-on- year, while investment trust holdings increased 36.8%, making them the main contributors to overall asset growth. The growth rate of total household financial assets reached its highest level since 1989. In addition, rising interest rates have encouraged greater household investment in Japanese government bonds (JGBs). Household JGB holdings increased 29% year-on- year to ¥22 trillion, with little sign of a slowdown in the pace of accumulation. As interest rates are expected to continue rising, household demand for JGBs is likely to remain strong, and we believe household JGB holdings are highly likely to exceed ¥30 trillion in the coming years. The household sector is therefore expected to play an increasingly important role in financing government borrowing. Overall, the expansion of household financial assets should provide support for private consumption going forward through positive wealth effects. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 18 September 2026 5 Will three hikes be enough to get inflation back to target? Our base case of a modest 75bp hiking cycle is premised on our view that i) the underlying inflation overshoot is also modest (50bp), and ii) supply disruptions should roll off the y/y rate in coming quarters. But the risk is that 75bp of hikes might not be enough. One concern is that wages might re-accelerate if the u-rate keeps falling. Given how well the economy is already performing, this could set off a substantial demand boom, which would call for even higher policy rates. A more pernicious scenario is that supply-driven inflation might remain stubbornly high. For example, there might be a lot more inflation in the pipeline due to the Iran conflict than we are accounting for in our base case. This would leave the Fed with a difficult choice: either accept a few more years of above-target inflation, or put more pressure on aggregate demand than has been needed to hit the target in the past, risking a recession. Either choice would tarnish Warsh’s legacy. We’ll see.

LLC Banks and AI: Fee Opportunities and Efficiency Gains Following our June review of how investment-grade non-financial firms discuss AI, we assess US and European bank commentary in earnings calls and other disclosures. Our key conclusion is that AI is likely to be credit-positive for banks through two channels. records.text: US Economics Weekly18 September 2026 ab 8 Fiscal policy - deadlines and deficits Congress has a lot on its plate. A recently passed continuing resolution keeps the government funded until December 11 buying a little more time. But, as well as FY 2027 appropriations, federal surface transportation programs from the infrastructure investment and jobs act (IIJA) are set to expire December 11 too. The House has passed the BUILD America 250 Act but there has been little progress in the Senate. This reauthorization covers ~$500bn of spending for critical infrastructure – roads, bridges, transit, and rail. Beyond that, the debt ceiling is set to bind in early 2027, the midterms could add uncertainty to the unfinished budget process, and further out the exhaustion of the Social Security trust fund looms in 2032. That is in the next Presidential term, the four years starting in 2028, and the term for Senators elected in 2026. Against this busy legislative backdrop, the federal budget deficit is running around 6.3% of GDP at a time when economic growth is robust and the labor market near full employment. This is essentially unseen in the history of the United States. All the while debt outstanding has surpassed $40 trillion and is on course to rise from the current 100% of GDP to breach 120% of GDP by 2036. Importantly, we expect the Bank to emphasise that the medium- term inflation outlook is "virtually unchanged", despite firmer near-term price dynamics. Taking comfort from hawkish peers Since June, higher energy prices have contributed to a more hawkish global policy backdrop, prompting major central banks (aka FED and ECB) to tighten rates. Markets have consequently repriced interest-rate expectations across jurisdictions, including Switzerland. But while recent energy price trends create upside risks to inflation, we believe the SNB will remain comfortably on hold. First, the inflation outlook does not warrant tighter policy, given Switzerland's comparatively low rate and a medium-term profile consistent with the SNB's price target range. Second, after prolonged upward pressure on the franc, the SNB is likely to welcome the CHF's summer depreciation and wider policy-rate differentials should limit renewed pressures. The resilience has come increasingly through Hormuz, where flows, including ship-to-ship transfers in Omani waters, have climbed to 10.4 mbd (Figure 4). On a 10-day average, flows out of Fujairah have reached 3.4 mbd, with Oman exports running at around 2.1 mbd and Red Sea flows averaging 2.1 mbd. Red Sea flows, however, are weakening. The last crude tanker loaded on September 12, although product loadings have continued at around 0.5 mbd in recent days. The most notable pivot has come from Saudi Arabia. Satellite data indicate Saudi oil moving through Hormuz averaged 2.9 mbd over the past six days, up from just 0.7 mbd in August (excluding ship-to-ship transfers). As a result, total Saudi exports reached 5 mbd on a 10-day moving average on Septeber 15. Why didn’t Saudi Arabia do this earlier? Most likely because it didn’t need to. That said, we view these primarily as risk scenarios rather than our baseline. Indeed, there is also a plausible case that the Committee is overestimating the underlying strength of demand. With GDP growth estimated at just 1.8% in the first half of 2026, the median participant is effectively assuming growth close to 3% in the second half of the year. To our eye, that appears somewhat aggressive given prevailing fundamentals. A similar argument applies to inflation, where we suspect many participants are overly pessimistic about the pace at which PCE inflation can return toward target. If we are right on these fronts, the Committee's appetite for rate recalibration could be satiated as we move through 2027. For now, however, the more important message from September's meeting is that policymakers appear increasingly concerned that policy has not yet become sufficiently restrictive and increasingly willing to recalibrate further if inflation fails to return to target clearly and at sufficient speed. records.text: US Economics Weekly18 September 2026 ab 28 S&P Global manufacturing and services PMIs (Sep flash), 9:45 AM We expect that the S&P Global manufacturing PMI was unchanged at 53.9 in the preliminary September data, signalling continued modest growth after being essentially unchanged in August. The new orders component, which carries the highest weight in the index (30%) likely moderated. In August, the new orders index edged down 0.1 points to 54.1, and we expect little change in September. We expect continued downward pressure from the supplier delivery times index, which accounts for 15% of the headline index. In contrast to the ISM methodology, the S&P Global PMI calculation inverts the supplier delivery times component, so longer delivery times cause the overall index to fall and effectively reduce the composite score. We expect that the S&P Global services PMI was unchanged at 56.5 in the preliminary September data. In August, the index rose 1.9 points to 56.5, marking a third straight month of gains since April. The business activity component in the ISM services composite was also upbeat in August, up 1.9 points to 55.3, comfortably above 50. Note that the S&P Global services headline index measures only business activity, unlike composite indexes such as the ISM composites or the S&P Global manufacturing index. records.text: Credit Implications: Reaffirming Our Overweight Stance on Banks AI adoption reinforces our constructive view on the banking sector. While the opportunity is more pronounced in the US, we think banks in both the US and Europe stand to benefit relative to non-financial firms in their respective markets. Banks can capture advisory, underwriting, syndication and asset-management fees from the AI capex cycle while generally limiting retained long-dated infrastructure credit and duration risk. AI-related efficiency gains and cost discipline should also support further improvement in efficiency ratios (Exhibit 12). We therefore reiterate our overweight recommendation on banks vs. non-financial sectors, particularly technology. USD bank spreads have outperformed technology year to date, and we expect this relative performance to continue (Exhibit 13). The key consideration is the divergent trajectory for leverage and supply: technology companies are utilizing their significant balance sheet flexibility to fund AI capex, contributing to a material increase in debt issuance. Technology now accounts for roughly 20% of USD IG gross supply this year, up from around 5% in 2024 (Exhibit 14). By contrast, we see little indication that banks are increasing leverage materially. Record USD IG bank supply reflects opportunistic issuance into tight spreads and, at the margin, AI-related growth in balance-sheet-intensive activities, including prime-brokerage financing of AI-related equity trading

Recent SEK weakness, stronger growth data, a robust September Business Survey and higher energy prices could justify somewhat higher policy-rate projections. Even so, we think the hurdle for delivering a materially more hawkish message than currently priced remains high, limiting the scope for SEK-positive surprises. For Norges Bank, markets are pricing 11bp next week and 29bp by year-end, while we continue to expect an extended hold. This leaves NOK exposed to downside risks in the near term. Norges’ hawkish bias has been a key driver of NOK strength this year, meaning a hold, if accompanied by softer communication, could turn an important tailwind into a drag. That said, upside risks remain meaningful, as the possibility of a surprise hike cannot be dismissed. Beyond next week's meetings, our medium-term bias remains bullish SEK and bearish NOK for three reasons: 1) The Swedish economy is beginning to accelerate while the Norwegian economy is slowing. 2) We expect rate differentials to move in SEK's favour. 3) European resilience together with lower energy prices next year should put downward pressure on NOKSEK. Near term, however, uncertainty around the Middle East keeps us cautious on expressing that view through the pair.

So we don’t think rates will reach the peak of 4.75% (unless things materially worsen), which the optimal policy path under the adverse scenario points to and which markets are pricing. QT decision adds more predictability to the QT process The MPC published a multi-year plan for its QT decision. It decided to reduce the stock of UK gilts held for monetary policy purposes to zero through a multi-year plan, such that the remaining stock is unwound at an annual average pace of £46bn by Sept. 2034, through annual sales of £20bn alongside maturing gilts. They have also set a high hurdle to future changes to the unwind path (such as severe gilt market stress or if Bank Rate is insufficient to meet the inflation target). Overall, the BoE has doubled down on making QT operate in the background, rather than an active policy tool. At the same time, pausing of active sales for potentially the next six months and selling bonds directly to the government were taken as a positive signal for the gilt market ahead of the Autumn Budget.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Oil Tracker: Running Out of Buffers The renewed pressure on energy prices has dragged the world into the seventh month of this prolonged energy price shock. Historically, episodes of acute geopolitical or physical supply disruption have mostly lasted 3–6 months, with the notable exception of the 1978– 79 oil shock and its aftermath. As buffers such as higher U.S. exports, weaker Chinese imports, and ample inventories begin to fade, we update our oil tracker to highlight developments and trends that matter for U.S. economic growth. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) have fallen further, while both U.S. crude oil imports and exports have remained on an upward trend. Crude oil prices have continued to rise, while diesel margins have widened further. Prices: higher crude spot prices, wider diesel margins The latest spot prices, as of September 15, were $107.02 per barrel for WTI in Cushing, Oklahoma, and $130.80 per barrel for Brent in Europe. We convert diesel and gasoline prices to a per-barrel basis for a better comparison: diesel was at $230.78 per barrel, while gasoline was at $180.37 per barrel. The gap between gasoline and crude oil prices has remained broadly unchanged, whereas the gap between diesel and crude oil prices has continued to widen since early July. records.text: Canada Economics Weekly 18 September 2026 Citi Research 2 The Fed raised rates this week after an abrupt shift in expectations over the last month due to rising oil prices and a stronger August inflation reading. Of course, BoC officials also shifted more hawkish at the September decision to leave rates unchanged, highlighting upside risks for inflation from higher for longer energy costs. The summary of deliberations of the September decision this week did little to change our views that officials will ultimately not raise rates this year. Most importantly, the summary clarified that “if higher energy prices did spill over into other components of the CPI, members agreed that it could require a monetary policy response to prevent broad-based inflation from setting in. ” Headline inflation will remain strong at least in the next few data releases. But we continue to expect little evidence of energy price pass through to core inflation, including in critical September CPI data released ahead of the October decision. If evidence of pass through is the criteria for rate hikes, and core inflation remains around 2%, market pricing of ~ 35bp of hikes this year and 100bp through mid- 2027 looks to be too much in our view. The index ratio resets on the 10th of each month to the CPI print from three months earlier, with daily interpolation between reset dates. The 10 September–10 October change is therefore already fixed at +0.39%, based on the rise in the index from 101.7 in June to 102.1 in July; Friday’s release will set the 10 October–10 November interval. A 1.7% YoY outcome, equivalent to an index level of 102.0, would imply a -0.1% monthly change. This would be followed by the seasonally strong 0.5–0.6% increase in October CPI, released on 20 November and reflected in the interval beginning 10 December. Against the 0.163% monthly accrual priced by 10y BEI at 1.95%, near-term inflation carry is already firmly positive. On 2024–25 seasonality, the cumulative six-month increase is 0.7–1.8%, versus 0.98% priced. The BoJ decision is due later the same day. records.text: conomics perspective, the French outlook is complicating very fast. Growth weakness in 2026 is more pronounced than elsewhere (Exhibit 20 for 2026 consensus growth expectations). We have cut our forecasts to 0.4% for this year and 0.8%, resp, in early September. The blend of cyclical weakness and higher exogenously driven inflation creates additional challenges for already strained public finances. We continue to expect a 5.3% deficit this year and 5.6% next, although energy price moves and financing conditions create additional risks to the growth, inflation and deficit outlook. Below are a few rules of thumb (see also note: Euro Area Viewpoint: France: it’s hard to be upbeat): • Standard fiscal multipliers suggest every 1ppt change in GDP growth would affect the cyclical deficit by around 0.4% of GDP. If growth recovers next year, we should see some improvement from that, although it risks to be less than currently thought. • A 100bp increase in headline inflation for a year can raise the deficit by 0.2-0.3% via inflation indexed bonds. In the following year, fiscal expenditures (pensions or select social security) could rise more than fiscal revenues unless the government decides otherwise. That dichotomy is particularly pronounced during exogenous (ie energy price shocks rather than endogenous inflation strength. • Debt concerns fuel rates fuel debt concerns: the French court of auditors estimated in June that a sustained 50bp rise in OAT yields would raise debt servicing

At the time, some clients argued that Warsh might regret having gotten the job given the political challenges of raising rates, particularly before the midterms. But after the September hike, we are sticking with our out-of-consensus call for two more 25bp increases in October and December, followed by an extended pause. Part of our reasoning is that the September hike is looking increasingly good for Warsh’s legacy so far. For one, the rate hike alleviates concerns that Warsh is not politically independent. Additional increases would end that conversation for good. For another, by hiking at just his third meeting as Fed Chair, Warsh can absolve himself of the inflation problem, while also taking credit for any disinflation in coming months. We expect the BEA’s methodological revisions and the rolling off of tariff and Iran effects from y/y inflation to push the core PCE toward 2.5% by the middle of next year (Exhibit 1). None of this would be a function of rate hikes, but the optics would be favorable for Warsh because he took action and the previous regime didn’t. records.text: On the back of the Chevron and ENI announcements in Venezuela, our updated Top Projects modelling shows Venezuelan crude reaching c.1.9 mboed by 2030 (+945 kboed vs 2025), with additional upside from the North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) JV which was granted 100-year concessions on 17 fields with c.65 bn bbl reserves. Across the majors, Chevron is targeting 600 kboed from 280 kboed today under a $7bn 5-year plan, ENI has secured a 25-year licence over c.35 bn bbl of certified oil in place at Junin-5, Repsol plans to triple oil production by 2028 and GeoPark aims to ramp Bare to c.90 kboed by 2038. On gas, we see c.140 mboed added on Dragon (Shell) and Loran (BP/XRG) with potential FID in 2027E/28E, feeding the existing Trinidad Atlantic LNG plant. On an NPV-at-15% basis, we see the largest value in Venezuelan assets for Chevron ($6.4bn), ENI ($4.8bn) and Repsol ($1.9bn), with potential Dragon/Loran FID derisking further value for Shell ($0.3bn) and BP ($0.1bn). On the economics side, the new fiscal regime (c.56% government take under LOH 2026) has materially improved project-level economics with an oil breakeven of c.$58/bbl, placing Venezuela in the 2nd quartile of the cost curve (below the 50th percentile at $64.5/bbl). records.text: M Idea 2 Detailed Musings Two phases of household deleveraging Housing-led deleveraging, 2H21 to 1H23. The property downturn that began in mid-2021 fundamentally altered the household leverage cycle. The first phase of deleveraging, from 2021 to mid-2023, was primarily a housing-price shock. As expectations for housing appreciation declined, the incentive to take on additional leverage weakened sharply. Balance-sheet metrics reflected a shock-driven, largely passive adjustment. Debt accumulation slowed and the debt-service burden eventually stabilized as interest rates fell, but the liability-to-asset ratio continued to rise. Confidence-led deleveraging, from mid-2023. Household credit stabilized briefly in early 2023 as the economy reopened and property transactions recovered, but subsequently resumed its decline despite two years of policy easing, lower mortgage rates, and relaxed purchase restrictions. The weakness also broadened. Short-term consumer lending has remained persistently soft and increasingly contractionary, despite improvements in both the debt-to-income ratio and debt-service ratio. In this context, the primary constraint on household borrowing appears to be demand rather than affordability. Persistent housing weakness has been compounded by deteriorating labor-market expectations and weaker expected income growth, pushing desired debt levels below the existing stock of household debt. Since it had also raised rates in June, this represented a marked acceleration from roughly one hike every six months to about one every three months. It was the first time in 36 and a half years, since March 1990, that the BoJ had delivered hikes at such an interval. Two Board members nominated by PM Takaichi dissent, as expected As we expected, Board Members Asada and Sato voted against the decision (7–2). In a Reuters interview on 7 July, he said that he would need to see demand-driven inflation accompanied by wage growth before supporting another hike. Super El Niño is likely emerging Current weather conditions suggest this El Niño could rank among the strongest on record. Pacific Ocean temperatures are already around 1.4°C above long-term averages, suggesting this may be among the most significant El Niño occurrences observed in recent decades. While no two El Niño events are the same, El Niño often means hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires. We do not find a material impact on headline inflation We measure the impact of El Niño on macroeconomic variables with the Vector Autoregression framework also used in Global Economic Viewpoint: El Niño risks are building. Our results indicate that El Niño may lower GDP, and while there may be some modest headline disinflationary pressure, we do not find any statistically significant effect on inflation overall. This likely reflects the fact that the GDP drag is concentrated in agriculture and trade-exposed sectors, while other parts of the economy provide an offsetting boost, such as construction which benefits from drier conditions. Another step in the BoJ's balance sheet normalization Alongside the release of its statement, the BoJ unanimously decided to revise its Funds- Supplying Operations to Support Financing for Climate Change Responses, including changes to the loan-rate calculation methodology and the introduction of a cap on the total amount of loans available under the operation. The measure can be viewed as a de facto additional step toward monetary policy normalization. Notably, both dovish Board members, Asada and Sato, who opposed the September 25bp rate hike, voted in favor of the revisions to the funds-supplying operation. This suggests that while the two members remain cautious about further policy rate hikes, they do not necessarily object to balance sheet normalization itself. Specifically, the loan rate will no longer be based on the IOER as of the date of loan disbursement. Instead, it will be linked to the average IOER during the period in which the loans are extended. In addition, the BoJ introduced caps on lending under the operation, with aggregate lending capped at ¥50 trillion and borrowing by each counterparty limited to ¥10 trillion. The government says that it adopted a fixed base year approach in order to maintain the stability and predictability of the budget. Basing the target on each year’s GDP would cause the defense budget to fluctuate annually in line with economic conditions. Furthermore, future changes in the GDP base year or definition would affect the budget amount as well. Such swings could disrupt long-term plans for equipment procurement and payment, which could adversely affect the nation’s defense capability. Australia & New Zealand: Weathering El Niño El Niño often means hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires, posing a downside growth risk and upside inflation risk. Nine of the ten driest winter-spring periods on record for Eastern Australia occurred in El Niño years, raising drought risk across key agricultural regions. But we find no material effect on headline inflation, likely reflecting offsetting forces within the CPI basket. While drier conditions may push food prices higher, they also tend to lower construction costs as less rain supports faster building completion times. New Zealand is more exposed than Australia, in our view. Agriculture accounts for 5% of GDP and food carries a 19% weight in the CPI basket (vs 2% and 13% in Australia). As the most agriculture-exposed economy in the G10, New Zealand's transmission channel is primarily negative growth rather than positive inflation, with reduced pasture growth curbing milk production and dairy export earnings. Week ahead In the coming week, we turn our focus to monetary policy meeting in Indonesia, as well as August inflation data in Singapore. In Indonesia, We expect BI to keep the policy rate unchanged and justified on the basis that baseline inflation outlook remains manageable. records.text: Our review of the eight largest US and ten largest public European banks suggests that direct retained balance-sheet exposure to AI infrastructure remains limited so far. These banks account for roughly 50% of US bank debt outstanding in the Bloomberg USD credit index, and 40% of European banks in the EUR IG corporate credit index. So far and based on our review, only one US bank disclosed direct lending to data-center projects, while another highlighted a strategic partnership related to the AI buildout (Exhibit 6). Most other banks discussed AI capex in broad commercial terms. European banks were somewhat more forthcoming on specific facilities, but overall disclosures suggest that direct exposure remains modest (at least for now). The Chicago Fed supervisory data support this conclusion: direct outstanding exposure to AI-adjacent sectors among large US banks represents just 0.8% of total bank assets, or roughly 9% of Tier 1 capital, rising to 25% when undrawn commitments are included. However, this likely understates banks’ broader AI-related balance-sheet exposure. Beyond direct lending to data centers and hyperscalers, banks may provide C&I lending to suppliers expanding capacity for the AI infrastructure buildout, as well as prime-brokerage and other financing to clients trading AI-related equities. Such activity is less likely to be disclosed explicitly as AI-related lending, but could become a more meaningful source of balance-sheet usage as the capex cycle broadens.

These solutions improve situational awareness, enable earlier identification of risks and support faster responses to emerging disruptions. • Climate risk modelling and geospatial analytics are becoming increasingly mainstream. Companies are developing platforms that combine geospatial mapping, predictive modelling and scenario analysis to assess exposure to hazards such as flooding, heat stress and sea-level rise for organisations that seek to better understand physical climate risks. • Digital twins and predictive infrastructure modelling are improving resilience. Virtual replicas of physical assets combined with real-time data and predictive analytics support operational optimisation, maintenance planning and long-term infrastructure investment decisions. Governor Ueda preserves policy flexibility with both hawkish and dovish remarks At his post-MPM press conference, Governor Ueda appeared to deliberately mix hawkish and dovish remarks to maximize future policy optionality. First, he characterized underlying inflation’s approach toward 2% as a “change in the policy phase. ” Although the substance of his remarks was nothing new, they left markets with a hawkish impression and may arm the BoJ with the logic for another rate hike after a short interval. He then said that, although financial conditions remain accommodative, the degree of accommodation is gradually diminishing as rates rise, making it necessary to carefully assess the cumulative effects going forward. He also said that abrupt rate hikes that could trigger major adjustments in lending or asset values should be avoided. Overall, our impression is that, even if the next hike comes sooner than the previous six-month interval, the BoJ itself does not yet have a firm view on its timing. El Niño pushing food prices higher can add an inflationary tail risk to an already sensitive inflation environment. Production in agricultural products such as wheat depends on rainfall conditions. The El Niño event introduces significant downside risk to production, as the event may result in drier-than average conditions across major wheat-producing areas in Eastern Australia. New Zealand: More exposed to El Niño The impact on New Zealand is likely to be stronger than the rest of the G10 countries, given New Zealand’s economic growth being more reliant on its dairy and meat production. The agriculture sector is the most exposed to El Niño, with a heterogenous impact on weather conditions between the east and west coast. Droughts occur in the eastern region, while floods can occur on the west coast. Why This El Niño Matters for New Zealand New Zealand’s location and economic structure means that the likely impact differs to Australia.
